title: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra review: the top dog of folding Androids
description:
With great software and battery for two days, the pricey svelte folder strikes best balance between phone and tablet
Samsung’s top folding phone for 2026 is its first to carry the “Ultra” moniker in its name, packing a much bigger battery and better cameras into the thin and light body of a book-style foldable.
The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra continues from where the exquisite Z Fold 7 left off last year. With its svelte chocolate bar dimensions opening into a square tablet, the Ultra sits above the new passport-shaped Z Fold 8 as Samsung’s top model. Costing £1,899 (€2,199/$2,099.99/A$2,999), it is a lot of money to pay for a phone, regardless of how many other devices it can theoretically replace in your pocket.
fullText:
With great software and battery for two days, the pricey svelte folder strikes best balance between phone and tablet

Samsung’s top folding phone for 2026 is its first to carry the “Ultra” moniker in its name, packing a much bigger battery and better cameras into the thin and light body of a book-style foldable.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra continues from where the exquisite Z Fold 7 left off last year. With its svelte chocolate bar dimensions opening into a square tablet, the Ultra sits above the new passport-shaped Z Fold 8 as Samsung’s top model. Costing £1,899 (€2,199/$2,099.99/A$2,999), it is a lot of money to pay for a phone, regardless of how many other devices it can theoretically replace in your pocket.

The Ultra sticks with the tried and tested form of its many Z Fold predecessors, and is almost identical to the Fold 7 physically. Weighing 215g and being only 8.9mm thick when closed, it is about the same as a large normal slab phone. The tall and super-bright outside screen makes easy work of phone-type tasks such as messaging, calls and mapping.

Open up the Ultra like a book to reveal the 8in OLED tablet screen, which is notably crisper and brighter than previous models, with a new anti-reflective coating that makes it easy to see in direct sunlight.

Browsing or reading books is particularly satisfying, while videos look great but have large letterboxing black bars top and bottom. The stereo speakers, when held in landscape, are good for watching TV without headphones.

The crease is less visible where the display folds but is still noticeable when the screen is off or you run your finger over it, and the necessarily softer material picks up fingerprints easily and needs more care than a traditional hardened glass smartphone.

Main screen: 8in QXGA+ 120Hz (422ppi) Amoled flexible display

Cover screen: 6.5in FHD+ 120Hz (422ppi) Amoled

Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy

Operating system: One UI 9 based on Android 17

Camera: 200+50+10MP rear with 3x telephoto; 10MP+10MP selfie cameras

Connectivity: 5G, dual sim, esim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, UWB, GNSS

Water resistance: IP48 (1.5 metres for 30 minutes)

Dimensions folded: 158.4 x 72.8 x 8.9mm

Dimensions unfolded: 158.4 x 143.2 x 4.1mm

The Ultra has two meaningful upgrades on the inside. The latest Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip has plenty of power for multitasking and demanding tasks, while a 13.6% larger capacity battery powers the phone through about two days of use. That is with the screens used for more than four hours each across a mix of wifi and 5G for browsing, messaging, taking notes, work and shooting photos, matching some of the longest-lasting folders available.

Gaming and more intensive tasks hit the battery harder, but most people will only need to charge the Ultra every other day.

The Ultra runs the same One UI 9 software built on the latest Android 17 as the Fold 8. It is the best available for folding screens, allowing you to do more with the form while remaining a polished, customisable and refined experience.

The Ultra can run up to three apps in a split-screen grid at once, plus more as floating windows, which can be handy for messaging while watching videos. Flex mode pushes the app or video to the top half of the screen when partly folded like a tiny laptop. You can have separate home screens for the phone and tablet displays, and choose whether or not to continue using apps on the outside when you shut the phone.

The Now Bar works great for putting live scores, music controls and other ongoing tasks on the bottom of the lock screen or in the status bar. The Ultra also has some of the better AI tools available, including Google’s Gemini and a proactive suggestion tool called Now Nudge from the S26, which has been expanded for One UI 9.

The Ultra will receive Android and security updates until 31 July 2033.

The Ultra has five cameras: a 10-megapixel selfie camera in each screen that is great for video calls; and three cameras on the back.

The main 200MP rear camera is little changed from last year’s model and remains the best of the bunch, capable of shooting fantastic photos across a range of lighting conditions. By default it captures photos at 12MP but can shoot at 50MP or the full 200MP with a quick tap of button. It also manages a very good 2x crop zoom for a bit of magnification.

The new 50MP ultra-wide camera is a big improvement on previous models, capturing brighter, more detailed photos, particularly in lower light settings. It also handles macrophotography well, producing excellent, highly detailed closeup shots.

The 10MP 3x telephoto camera is the weakest of the bunch. It can shoot good photos with a bit of work, but it falls far short of modern rivals on zoom and quality, particularly with indoor lighting. Digital zoom takes over for further magnification up to 30x, which starts to fall apart beyond 10x.

The cameras shoot great video, too, with a range of modes available including the impressive horizontal lock stabilisation feature from the S26 Ultra.

The battery has an expected lifespan of at least 1,200 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is generally repairable. Inside screen repairs cost about £600. Samsung offers a self-repair programme, as well as Care+ accidental damage insurance that reduces the cost of repairs to £50.

The Fold 8 is made from 14.4% recycled materials by weight. Samsung offers trade-in and recycling schemes for old devices, and publishes environmental impact in its reports.

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs from £1,899 (€2,199/$2,099.99/A$2,999).

For comparison, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 costs £1,699, the S26 Ultra costs £1,279, the Honor Magic V6 costs £1,999.99 and the Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold costs £1,299.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is the best folding phone available. It is not a radical upgrade on last year’s excellent Z Fold 7 and does not really deserve the “Ultra” branding, but the longer, two-day battery life is very welcome.

The form factor is great: easy to use as a regular phone when closed, plus an 8in internal screen that is brighter, crisper and much easier to use outdoors than before. The square tablet screen is great for multitasking, browsing and apps while being big enough to make watching video a good experience despite needing large letterboxing black bars.

The triple camera on the back is generally capable and does not feel like a large downgrade from normal flagship phones, even if the 3x telephoto camera is a bit weak. The Ultra has the top Android processor from Qualcomm with plenty of performance for anything you would want to do.

While you can get similar performance and battery life with better cameras and a less visible crease from some rivals, the Fold Ultra’s excellent, adaptable software is simply better and will be kept up to date until at least 31 July 2033.

Samsung has given wealthy buyers a choice of shape for its book-style foldable phones this year, but while the squatter Fold 8 seems better for video on paper, the Fold 8 Ultra is the one to get.

Pros: super thin and light, just like a regular phone when closed, great tablet screen, powerful multitasking with top performance, two-day battery life, water resistance, good set of cameras.

Cons: extremely expensive, no dust resistance, more fragile than a regular device and costly to repair, weak zoom camera compared with the very best normal phones, not a big upgrade on last year’s Z Fold 7.

title: Peggy Flanagan vows to 'rip ICE apart' after toppling moderate Dem in key Senate battle
description: Peggy Flanagan defeated Angie Craig in Minnesota's Democratic primary, backed by Bernie Sanders and Ilhan Omar in a growing progressive proxy war.
fullText:
Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who scored an impressive win in Minnesota's Democratic primary for Senate, wants to blow up Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after two slayings rattled her state earlier this year. 

"Now let's talk about Donald Trump's out of control ICE force," Flanagan said during her victory speech Tuesday night. "We need to rip ICE apart and stop them from terrorizing our communities. And I know this. I know that we can fix our broken immigration system, secure the border, and create a real pathway to citizenship that aligns with our values."

Flanagan is another progressive insurgent challenging the status quo in the Democratic Party and handed Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., another defeat in the progressive proxy war in her decisive victory over Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn.

Republicans Get The Democrat They Wanted As Socialist Abdul El-sayed Wins Michigan Senate Primary

Flanagan, like other progressives in the hunt for a position of power in Congress, has honed her left-leaning bona fides by backing Medicare for all and pushing an end to military aid to Israel.

She's vowed to go after ICE on the campaign trail in the wake of the two deadly immigration enforcement-related shootings of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota, and used Craig's support of legislation, like the Laken Riley Act, as a political cudgel to build a distinction between the two of them.

Those positions have earned her the backing of progressive heavyweights like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and even Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., whose decision to retire from the Senate opened up the contest. 

Notably, Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., who is running for governor, has not weighed in on the race so far.

Craig, who was viewed as the safer, more moderate pick, had the backing of the Democratic old-guard, including Schumer.

Big Money Propels Dem Megachurch Pastor To Victory In Longshot Kansas Senate Bid

Republicans are licking their chops, too, at Schumer getting handed another loss.

"Morale among Chuck Schumer's establishment is at an all-time low, and Bernie Sanders' socialist flank is filling the gap with candidates like Peggy Flanagan and Abdul El-Sayed," Bernadette Breslin, a spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told Fox News Digital.

And it's also brought reams of cash into the race. Craig has raised nearly $13 million this cycle, according to filings from the Federal Election Commission, while Flanagan has raked in just shy of $7 million.

"Peggy Flanagan is about bringing about real change, standing up to the big money interests," Sanders told "Face the Nation" on Sunday. "There is a reason why the super PACs and the billionaires are flooding Minnesota with all kinds of money. Same thing as Michigan."

Republicans see Flanagan's candidacy in the same vein as Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who last week similarly squeaked out a narrow win over Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., who, like Craig, has Schumer's backing.

Bomb-thrower Dem Makes Shocking Promise To Kick Schumer To Curb During Senate Debate

They also have built-in messaging against her: Flanagan was Walz's right hand as the Minnesota fraud scandal rippled across the airwaves and nation. While the scandal killed his prospects of running for reelection as governor, it has so far not kneecapped Flanagan's candidacy. And Walz hasn't waded into the endorsement game in the Senate contest, either.

They're confident that national Republicans' candidate of choice, former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, will be the one to turn Minnesota red. There's also the possibility that Flanagan, who has not raked in the same level of cash that Craig did, may become a resource drain for other key races on Democrats' scorecard.

"Minnesota and Michigan being in play was not on Chuck Schumer's bingo card this cycle," a GOP operative told Fox News Digital. "It remains to be seen which battleground(s) Democrats will have to pull resources from to drag socialists like Peggy Flanagan and Abdul El-Sayed across the finish line in November."

And Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., when asked by CNN which races kept him up at night, said one contest gave him hope.

"The one thing that gets me excited when I think about this election cycle on the map is Minnesota," said Scott, the chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC). "I think Minnesota, we have a real shot with Michele Tafoya."

"What we know without question is, she is within a point of the lieutenant governor right now," he said. "So if we can continue to let her show the contrast between the two candidates, I think Michele Tafoya's the kind of Republican that can win."

title: Taiwan says it was hit by ‘abnormal’ AI-assisted cyber-attack
description:
Taiwan’s statement comes a day after reports that suspected China-linked hackers had carried out a first-of-a-kind breach
Taiwan says it detected AI-assisted cyber-attacks on government agencies that came from overseas last month, a new kind of threat that has been reported as “first-of-a-kind breach”.
The Ministry of Digital Affairs (MDA) said its cybersecurity monitoring units ‌detected the “abnormal attack” targeting government agencies, which began on 20 July. The National Institute of Cyber Security issued a series of warning alerts while it investigated.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Taiwan’s statement comes a day after reports that suspected China-linked hackers had carried out a first-of-a-kind breach

Taiwan says it detected AI-assisted cyber-attacks on government agencies that came from overseas last month, a new kind of threat that has been reported as “first-of-a-kind breach”.

The Ministry of Digital Affairs (MDA) said its cybersecurity monitoring units ‌detected the “abnormal attack” targeting government agencies, which began on 20 July. The National Institute of Cyber Security issued a series of warning alerts while it investigated.

The Financial Times quoted Dream – an Israeli AI company that detected the intrusion – as saying the attackers used open-source AI agents to build an autonomous hacking tool that behaved like a coordinated cyber team, describing it as a first-of-a-kind breach.

Dream was reported as saying that the tool compromised “at least 85 government user accounts, extracting more than 2,500 personnel records before expanding the attack to Taiwan’s nuclear safety agency and at least seven energy companies”.

Taiwan has in recent years complained about what it sees as China’s “hybrid warfare” – from daily military drills near the island to disinformation campaigns and cyber-attacks – as Beijing ramps up military and political pressure ⁠on the democratically governed island to force Taipei to accept its claims of sovereignty.

Though Taiwanese officials did not direct accusations at China, the FT on Wednesday reported that China-linked hackers were suspected. Dream did not attribute the attack to a specific group, but said the use of Simplified Chinese in internal communications linked to the hack meant there was a high probability the operator was connected to China, the FT reported.

Chinese cyber-attacks on Taiwan’s key infrastructure, from hospitals to banks, rose 6% in 2025 from the previous year to an average of 2.63m attacks a ⁠day, the island’s National Security Bureau said in January, adding some hacks were synchronised with military drills in “hybrid threats” to paralyse the island.

The investigation into the AI-assisted attack said it showed clear characteristics of an “overseas source”, with hackers employing a hybrid approach that combined manual operations with AI agent-assisted attacks, such as Open Claw, the MDA said.

“The relevant attack sources, methods, and scope of impact have all been fully investigated, and the affected units have successively completed their handling,” the ministry added.

In response to this new type of threat, the government has established protective guidelines and strengthened system monitoring to block attacks early, it said.

The statement did not mention China, and China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request ‌for comment on the attack.

Taiwan’s MDA and Chinese authorities did not comment on the earlier FT report.

The threat of AI-assisted hacking campaigns has ​been growing for years but ramped up dramatically ​over the past few months after top AI labs ​released models, such as Anthropic’s Mythos, which can rapidly conduct reconnaissance, identify vulnerabilities, and take advantage of them.

Cris Thomas, a ​researcher who works as a ‌security advocate at the code ​security company Semgrep, said the ​spy campaign was an illustration of just how quickly AI-assisted hackers could hit their mark.

Thomas cautioned against exaggerating the power of AI agents, however.

“There’s still a human in there somewhere. Somebody had to choose who to attack, had to establish an objective and give it a directive,” he said. “It’s not totally 100% autonomous. There was a capable operator in charge that did that.”

title: Zhu Rongji, Chinese premier who cajoled economy into modern era, dies at 97
description: Former Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji, who died on Wednesday aged 97, was never one to mince his words.
fullText:
BEIJING, Aug 12 (Reuters) - Former Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji, who died on Wednesday aged 97, was never one to mince his words.

When the four-volume selection of his speeches came out in 2011, they shocked readers with his description of "tofu dregs" flood dykes built by "parasites", ‌and erring bankers labelled as "half-wits".

It was little wonder that his blunt comments from his years in power became best-sellers, finding eager readers ‌in a nation whose then leaders were seen as wary and cautious, prone to often bland public pronouncements.

Yet the reaction to Zhu's speech selection from his time as vice premier from 1991 ​to 1998 and then as premier until early 2003 also reflected deeper anxieties coursing through China as it approached a transition that ushered in Xi Jinping as leader.

Reformist former officials and intellectuals held up the 2,042 pages of Zhu's words, many made public for the first time, as an unflattering mirror to the conservatism and conformism of current leaders. Magazine editors and internet users scoured the volumes for any comments that offer a message for the present.

Indeed, many of the problems that dogged ‌China's economy as Xi prepared to take power dominated "The ⁠Authentic Speeches of Zhu Rongji": local government debt and reckless bank loans, inflation and feverish urban growth, and corruption devouring public trust and coffers.

"Our country faces many potential crises that could erupt at any time," Zhu said early in 1998. "Ordinary people ⁠are discontent about us in many ways. Especially, there is corruption among officials, the gulf between rich and poor, and the way some local officials act like tyrants."

Zhu graduated from Beijing's elite Tsinghua University, joining the Communist Party in 1949, the same year Mao Zedong declared the People's Republic of China.

Sent to the countryside during the chaos ​of ​the Cultural Revolution, he gradually worked his way up through the ranks after being politically ​rehabilitated, and was appointed Shanghai mayor in 1987, overseeing its ‌first steps into becoming the global financial hub it is today.

Moving to Beijing in 1991 to work for the central government, he helped push the reforms that transformed China from a beleaguered hold-out against the collapse of Soviet-style Communism in the early 1990s to an emerging superpower with economic growth rates envied by other governments.

Zhu dragged back the Chinese economy from over-heating in the early 1990s, and then as premier pushed through reforms that shut or privatised many state-owned firms and laid off workers, wrenched tax power from local officials to the central government, and launched housing ownership reforms that gave birth to a feverish ‌real-estate boom.

Above all, Zhu coaxed and cajoled China's way into the World Trade Organization in ​2002 through gruelling negotiations. At the time, many Chinese officials feared he had made so ​many concessions to gain entry that China's economy would be hobbled.

Zhou Ruijin, ​a former senior editor of the People's Daily, the Communist Party's official newspaper, suggested in a 2011 interview that the leaders likely to succeed then-President Hu Jintao and then-Premier Wen Jiabao had much to learn from Zhu.

"The Zhu Rongji era was one of promoting big reforms, and it ​nurtured a group of brave risk-takers who were at ‌the forefront of pioneering a market economy," Zhou, a cheerleader for rapid market reforms in the 1990s, said in an interview with ​South Breeze Window, a historically pro-reform magazine published in south China.

"Today ... there is still potential for big steps in reform."

title: Man airlifted to hospital after being bitten by shark
description: The incident happened on board a small vessel off the coast of County Waterford in the Republic of Ireland on Tuesday.
fullText:
A man has been taken to hospital after a suspected shark bite on the south coast of Ireland on Tuesday.

Five people were on board a small boat which was about four miles off Ram Head, Ard

Ballycotton RNLI in Cork said it was called at 16:16 local time by the Dublin Coast Guard to assist a "five-metre pleasure craft" which had five people on board.

The man was winched on board the Irish Coast Guard's helicopter, Rescue 117 and taken to Cork University Hospital, where he remains.

After the alarm had been raised multiple agencies, including the Irish Coast Guard Helicopter Rescue 117, Ballycotton RNLI and Youghal RNLI had responded to the incident.

Ballycotton RNLI 's all-weather Trent-class lifeboat, The Austin Lidbury, was launched at 16:30 and thanks to "calm sea conditions and good visibility" arrived about 17:10.

However Youghal RNLI and Rescue 117 were already at the boat where the incident happened and the two lifeboats were on standby as the man was taken from the boat.

Ballycotton RNLI was back at the harbour at around 18:15 that evening, where the lifeboat was refuelled before the volunteer crew continued with their scheduled weekly training session.

"This was a well-coordinated multi-agency response, with Ballycotton RNLI, Youghal RNLI and Rescue 117 working together to ensure that the casualty received urgent medical assistance as quickly and safely as possible," said the coxswain (the person who is in charge of a boat) on duty, Eolan Walsh.

"Incidents such as this are a reminder that conditions at sea can change quickly and that anyone heading offshore should make safety a priority.

"Ensure your vessel is suitable for the conditions, wear a properly-fitted lifejacket or personal flotation device, carry a reliable means of communication, and make sure someone ashore knows your plans."

This is not the first time people have been bitten by sharks off the Irish coast.

In 2018, a Belfast man who was angling caught a Blue Shark and was bit while bringing it on board the angling boat.

His lower arm was seriously injured in an incident where he was helped by Crosshaven RNLI in Cork.

title: Police rescue 60 cats and kittens from abandoned sailboat off Washington beach after 6-day operation
description: Tacoma police spent six days rescuing 60 cats from an abandoned 40-foot sailboat off Owens Beach, with many animals found frightened and malnourished.
fullText:
An abandoned sailboat off a Washington beach was home to an unexpected crew: 60 cats and kittens, many of them some frightened and malnourished.

The Tacoma Police Department said the unusual rescue began Aug. 6 when its Marine Services Unit responded to reports of an abandoned 40-foot sailboat in the waters off Owen Beach.

Officers initially discovered more than 30 cats and kittens living in unsafe conditions aboard the vessel, with many appearing frightened and malnourished. Marine Services began coordinating with Animal Control and the department's Forensics Unit to safely remove the animals.

What initially appeared to be a rescue involving more than 30 cats eventually grew to 60 over the course of a rescue effort spanning six days.

Florida Man Allegedly Kills Family's Kittens In Front Of Teenage Daughter As Form Of Punishment: Officials

"That's a wrap! The final cat is off the boat. Fur real this time!" police wrote. "Final cat count: 60!"

Police said Animal Control was "as certain as they can be that all cats have officially disembarked."

"That's all for meow!" the department joked online.

Despite believing all 60 cats had been rescued, police said they would continue making trips to the boat this week as a precaution.

Hero Sheepdog Becomes Unlikely Rescue Partner After Unexpected Move Aids First Responders

"While we believe we have safely removed all of the cats from the boat, as any cat owner knows, cats are exceptionally good at hiding," police said. "Because there is always a possibility that a cat may remain onboard, our work isn't quite finished."

The department said the additional searches would be conducted under the authority of a search warrant.

Police said Marine Services has also begun the process of having the legally registered vessel moved.

Authorities asked people visiting Owen Beach or boating nearby to notify Animal Control if they spot another cat aboard the vessel, while warning members of the public not to attempt their own rescues.

Florida Mail Carrier Accused Of Snatching Pets On Route, Trapping 100-Plus Cats And Dogs In 'Hoarding' House

"We know many animal lovers in our community want to help, and we appreciate the concern for these cats," police said. "However, this remains an active criminal case. Our teams are working hard to protect the animals while also protecting the integrity of the investigation."

"PLEASE DO NOT BOARD THE VESSEL unless you are the legal owner," police added.

The warning followed an incident in which private cat rescue trapper Camille Sutherland told King 5 she boarded the vessel overnight and captured two cats, which she took to the Humane Society.

Sutherland told the outlet she was trying to help and believed authorities were taking too long to rescue the animals.

Police told KING 5 that the unauthorized boarding complicated their investigation into the vessel's owner.

Police have not announced any arrests or charges in connection with the case.

More than 40 of the 60 rescued cats were taken to the Humane Society for Tacoma & Pierce County, while the remaining animals were placed in foster homes in the area, according to KING 5.

title: Britain to swelter again as it looks poised for a record hot summer
description: Large parts of western Europe will be sweltering once again on Thursday, with Britain poised for its fifth heat wave of an exceptional summer that is expected to be the hottest on record.  Forecasters...
fullText:
LONDON (AP) — Large parts of western Europe will be sweltering once again on Thursday, with Britain poised for its fifth heat wave of an exceptional summer that is expected to be the hottest on record.

Forecasters are predicting the mercury to rise as high as 38 Celsius (100 Fahrenheit) in central and southeast England, falling just short of the August record of 38.5 C in 2003.

The Met Office said earlier this week that only average conditions were needed for the rest of August to beat last year's record for the hottest year.

For a country that's largely not equipped to deal with these levels of heat, it's been a particularly uncomfortable few weeks.

That's particularly true in hospitals where nurses have been known to collapse from heat exhaustion, according to the Royal College of Nursing.

"When nursing staff are collapsing, feeling dizzy, sick or even being admitted to the very hospitals they work in because their workplaces cannot handle the heat, it shows just how badly they are being failed," said RCN chief executive and general secretary Professor Nicola Ranger.

The bulk of the country is now officially in drought, heaping pressure on water resources for households, agriculture and the environment.

Southern Water, which oversees supplies in the south of England, has applied for a rare drought order which would ban businesses from nonessential water use, including cleaning cars and filling nondomestic swimming pools, saying an "exceptional" lack of rain has threatened supplies in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. Environment Secretary Angela Eagle will decide on the application, which would be the first such ban since May 2006.

Meanwhile, wildfires have been blazing uncontrollably, most notably this week in the New Forest in southern England. Some 1,017 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to data from the National Fire Chiefs Council, the same as last year's record-breaking total.

Though not on the level as those witnessed in France, Greece and Spain, they provide ample evidence of the need for the U.K. to adjust to a new reality.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will consider imposing a ban on disposable barbecues amid the risk of further wildfires as extreme heat continues to grip parts of the U.K.

"I do believe we need to get the message out loud and clear," he said. "People should not be using those barbecues outside at this moment in time."

title: Tlaib under fire for working to unseat two Jewish House Democrats in Florida: 'No coincidence'
description: Rashida Tlaib is rallying in Fort Lauderdale to back socialists challenging Jared Moskowitz and Debbie Wasserman Schultz in their primaries.
fullText:
Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., is being criticized by Florida's lone Jewish Republican in Congress as she works to unseat two fellow House Democrats.

Tlaib is appearing at a rally in Fort Lauderdale Friday held by left-wing groups in support of three congressional candidates, according to a flier posted on Instagram, including two socialists running to unseat Reps. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., and Debbie Wasserman Schultz, D-Fla.

"I think that it's no coincidence that she's coming to target two of the remaining Jewish Democrats," Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital.

Jeffries Declines To Back Wasserman Schultz As Black Leaders Revolt Over District Switch

"It won't be well received in Florida," he continued. "How it's received in a Democratic primary — look, the Democrats are lost. But I'm going to hope that Florida Democrats are smarter than national Democrats because the Jew hatred side of the Democratic Party is not good for America."

Tlaib has been a power player on the far left so far this election cycle as candidates linked to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) dominate establishment Democrats in key elections across the country.

But DSA-linked candidates have also been accused of criticism against Israel that approaches antisemitism, according to the group's opponents, while being sympathetic to terror groups like Hamas.

Tlaib, the first Palestinian American woman in Congress, has faced bipartisan criticism for her comments on Israel and Jewish people. The Michigan congresswoman has denied accusations of antisemitism.

Former Bernie Sanders Official Accuses Senator Of Pushing Most Antisemitic Candidates 'In A Generation'

But Fine said Tlaib was a "vocal supporter of Hamas" and said the far left was making Jews in America feel unsafe.

"I think the Democratic Party is lost, and I think it's dangerous. I don't know that it's lost and dangerous in Fort Lauderdale or Florida, but nationally, the kinds of people that the Democrats are nominating, these are people who do not love America," Fine said of the far-left surge.

"They hate it. They are here to destroy it, and no one embodies that better than Rashida Tlaib."

DSA-linked candidates have already toppled House Democrats in New York, Colorado and Michigan. Also in Michigan, socialist politician Abdul El-Sayed defeated establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens for the party's nomination for Senate.

Dems' Leftward Lurch Gets Legs As El-sayed's Michigan Senate Victory Sparks Party Debate

Tlaib campaigned with El-Sayed and other DSA candidates across the U.S.

Friday's rally is called Chomp the Oligarchy and is being hosted by progressive groups like Gen Z For Change and Florida Youth Justice Coalition.

Moskowitz and Wasserman Schultz's campaigns did not respond to requests for comment on Tlaib's appearance. Tlaib's campaign did not respond to a request for comment on Fine's remarks.

Tlaib and other Democrats have previously accused Fine of anti-Muslim racism.

Moskowitz, who represents Florida's 23rd Congressional District, is running for re-election in the 25th Congressional District, which was recently redrawn to give Republicans a better shot in the general race.

Wasserman Schultz is running in the newly redrawn 20th Congressional District, a majority-Black district that leans heavily Democratic, sparking backlash for potentially impacting the area's historically Black representation.

title: What to know from AP's report about pregnant women and babies dying in Nepal amid USAID cuts
description: The United States’ decision to slash its foreign aid program has led to an increase in deaths of pregnant women and babies in Nepal, The Associated Press has found.  The decision by U.S. President Don...
fullText:
GAUR, Nepal (AP) — The United States' decision to slash its foreign aid program has led to an increase in deaths of pregnant women and babies in Nepal, The Associated Press has found.

The decision by U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to eliminate the United States Agency for International Development last year gutted maternal and child health programs worldwide. In Nepal, the funding cuts led to the closure of nutrition and reproductive outreach programs designed to save mothers' and babies' lives.

The U.S. State Department says it still supports programs in Nepal aimed at improving maternal and child health. But health workers, government officials, aid workers and families in Nepal say the funding cuts have had a devastating and deadly impact on pregnant women and babies.

Here's what to know from AP's report on the fallout of the funding cuts:

The decision by the Trump administration to dissolve USAID — once the world's largest humanitarian donor — decimated nutrition programs for millions of pregnant women and children and left scores of birthing centers devoid of equipment, medicine and staff. The U.S. cuts, followed by foreign aid cuts from several other countries, forced 60 percent of women's organizations to reduce their services, according to the World Health Organization.

In Nepal, the funding cuts eliminated nutrition programs that provided supplements and food items to impoverished pregnant women, and closed a program that equipped birthing centers and trained nurses, midwives and outreach workers. Those workers regularly visited pregnant women's homes, explained the warning signs of complications and urged them to attend prenatal appointments, often escorting them there. That program reached 100,000 women and girls across Nepal in its first three years.

Because of cuts by the U.S. and other countries to foreign aid, the Gates Foundation has predicted that 2025 will be the first year this century where child deaths will increase.

In Nepal, the program closures meant many pregnant women have found it difficult to adequately feed themselves, and left them to navigate a medical system they struggle to trust or understand. As a result, pregnant women aren't identifying complications fast enough, leading to emergencies, health workers and government officials say.

"The number of deaths of mothers, young mothers, during delivery has really increased," says Mona Sherpa, country director for the aid group CARE Nepal, which lost more than half its funding from the U.S. cuts. "The expected number within a year is happening within four to six months."

Babies, too, have increasingly died since the program closures. In the village of Prempur Gonahi, for example, it took just 10 months — a touch longer than a typical pregnancy — for newborns to begin dying again after the U.S. cuts, says the officer in charge, Sadho Baitha.

Before CARE's program launched in Rautahat in December 2022, Baitha says, the village averaged 10 to 15 neonatal deaths per year. By 2024, records show, there were zero. But since the program's cancelation, newborns have begun dying again; the first was in December, and four more followed by March.

Yet many deaths linked to the funding cuts will remain invisible, in part because the cuts themselves left scores of mortality data collectors jobless. In some places, there is simply no one left to count people who died.

Most of the women helped by these canceled programs are poor, uneducated and isolated. Even if they make it to a doctor, they often struggle to understand what the doctor is saying.

The outreach workers who operated under CARE's program would frequently visit pregnant women's homes, escort them to prenatal appointments and act as a mediator between the women and their doctors to ensure nothing was lost in translation.

Kabita Mukhiya, for example, was a 20-year-old uneducated woman living in a poor village near the India border. When she was pregnant, she experienced excruciating stomach pains, severe swelling and delirium. She was also starving; the U.S.-funded nutrition supplements and food she received in a previous pregnancy had been eliminated by the funding cuts. And the outreach workers who once visited her village to help pregnant women had stopped coming.

Not realizing her symptoms constituted an emergency, Mukhiya suffered at home for weeks before her aunt took her to the hospital. By then, it was too late: Both she and her unborn baby died.

Mukhiya died from complications of eclampsia, with severe anemia contributing significantly -- both conditions that can often be identified and managed through regular prenatal care, health workers say.

Rajkumari Patel, who worked as an outreach worker under CARE's canceled program, says deaths like Mukhiya's were precisely what she and her colleagues had been trained to prevent.

"I would have asked her, 'Is the baby kicking? When did you last feel movement?' I would have checked for swelling in her hands and face. I would have looked at her eyes for signs of anemia," Patel says. "These are the signs I would have noticed in Kabita and said, 'This woman needs a hospital today -- not tomorrow.' Maybe we could have saved her life."

title: Fetterman says he won’t campaign against McCormick
description: Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) said he would not campaign against Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.) in 2030 if the Republican chooses to run for a second term.
fullText:
Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) said he would not campaign against Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.) in 2030 if the Republican chooses to run for a second term.

In remarks made to the Washington Examiner, Fetterman was asked whether he would support or oppose McCormick's potential run in four years.

"Well, I would absolutely never move against my friend," he said, referring to McCormick as a "great guy."

The two Pennsylvania senators represent just one of three states with split representation in the Senate. They have done media appearances together, co-sponsored bills, and in July, they filed a joint fundraising effort. The new political action committee, called Common Ground PA, is accepting donations from those who want to support both purple state senators.

"This group of donors value the collaboration exhibited by Senators McCormick and Fetterman for Pennsylvania and want to support both of them," a spokesperson told The Center Square, a local outlet.

McCormick also praised Fetterman on Sunday in an appearance on "The Cats Roundtable" with host John Catsimatidis.

"He's willing to stand up and call out the craziness that's happening in his party," the Republican said, citing wins in Democratic primaries for progressive candidates during the 2026 midterms. "It's made him unpopular with some of the people in his party."

McCormick added that he was "lucky to have a good partner in Pennsylvania," noting that he has had people attempt to stop his praise of the relationship with Fetterman.

The Democratic senator has been a critic of democratic socialism and progressivism with a major point being his opposition to candidates who are against Israel.

At the Hill Nation Summit, Fetterman said he had "no plans" to leave the Democratic party, but he said if the party turned its back on Israel, he would consider leaving.

"If our party ever becomes — and just makes it official — the anti-Israel party, that's when I would leave because that's been a moral clarity for me," he said.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said in late July that Republicans would "welcome" Fetterman into the party if he decides to leave the Democratic party.

title: Mamdani's team said NYPD would accompany his wife on Middle East vacation — cops say that's not true
description: The NYPD denied it would send officers to Syria and Lebanon with Rama Duwaji, contradicting Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office on the security detail.
fullText:
The New York Police Department (NYPD) will not provide a security detail to Mayor Zohran Mamdani's wife during her upcoming vacation to two terror hotspots in the Middle East, despite the mayor's office claiming otherwise.

"The NYPD does not send officers to countries with level 4 travel advisories for discretionary reasons such as personal travel," a spokesperson for the law enforcement agency told Fox News.

Mamdani's wife, Rama Duwaji, is planning to travel to Syria and Lebanon to visit family in September, according to the New York Post. Both of those countries are on the State Department's "Do Not Travel" list due to terrorism concerns.

Mamdani's Wife Co-hosts Luxe Muslim Retreat Casting Virgin Mary As 'Palestinian Woman' Under Occupation

The mayor's office had previously confirmed that Duwaji would have an NYPD security detail on the trip.

"Upon the strong recommendation of the NYPD, the first lady's security detail will be joining her when she travels to visit family in Syria and Lebanon," Mamdani's spokeswoman Dora Pekec reportedly said.

But later, as it became clear that the NYPD would not be making the overseas trek, the mayor chalked the confusion up to a staff "miscommunication" when asked about it by news outlet PIX11 on Tuesday.

NYPD Detectives' Endowment Association (DEA) President Scott Munro furiously slammed the implication that NYPD detectives would accompany the city's First Lady to the Middle East.

Mamdani Clashes With Democratic Socialists' Push To Abolish Police And Prisons

"Our detectives put themselves in harm's way every day protecting New Yorkers," said Munro. "The DEA would never remain silent if our members were asked to travel to a dangerous, off-limits foreign country for anything other than a legitimate law-enforcement or intelligence operation."

"Our detectives are needed here in New York City protecting residents and fighting crime," he added.

Mamdani has a long history of trashing the very police department he thought would accompany and provide security for his wife to the dangerous Middle Eastern countries on New York City taxpayer's dime.

"There is no negotiating with an institution this wicked & corrupt. Defund it. Dismantle it. End the cycle of violence," Mamdani said in reference to the NYPD in a viral 2020 post on X.

"We don't need an investigation to know that the NYPD is racist, anti-queer & a major threat to public safety," he said in another 2020 post, adding in a follow-up: "What we need is to #DefundTheNYPD."

Jon Stewart Presses Mamdani On Where He Breaks With Fellow Democratic Socialists On Prisons And Borders

"Queer liberation means defund the police," he said in yet another post.

The mayor, who has also faced scrutiny for his anti-Israel views and recently called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a "war criminal" while calling for his arrest, derogatorily linked the NYPD to the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF).

"We have to make clear that when the boot of the NYPD is on your neck, it's been laced by the IDF," Mamdani, who was a keynote speaker, said during a panel discussion at the Democratic Socialists of America's 2023 national convention.

During his campaign for mayor of the most populated U.S. city, Mamdani said the exact opposite, explicitly stating that he did not want to defund the police.

See It: Mamdani Booed Off Stage At New York City Pro-police Celebration: 'Walked Off In Shame'

Still, it appears there is no love lost between Mamdani and the NYPD.

Just last week, he was booed offstage when he tried to speak at a pro-police event in Staten Island.

Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani's office for comment.

title: Bihina saves four penalties as Cameroon upset Morocco to make Wafcon final
description: Cameroon's Michaely Bihina saves an extra-time penalty and three more spot kicks in a shootout to send her side though to the 2026 Wafcon final at the expense of host nation Morocco.
fullText:
Michaely Bihina was the heroine as the Cameroon goalkeeper saved an extra-time penalty and three more spot-kicks in a shootout to send her side though to the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations final at the expense of host nation Morocco.

The 22-year-old pushed away Fatima Tagnaout's attempt from 12 yards in the 118th minute to ensure the game in Rabat finished 0-0 after 120 minutes.

Bihina then brilliantly kept out efforts from Kenza Chapelle, Maryame Atiq and Sakina Ouzraoui to leave the Moulay Hassan Stadium in stunned silence.

Teenage Cameroon defender Maryam Nyadjou held her nerve to secure a 3-1 win on penalties for the Central Africans.

The Indomitable Lionesses will face Malawi in Sunday's final (19:00 GMT) after the southern Africans beat Algeria 3-1 earlier on Wednesday.

Cameroon's run to the final is all the more remarkable given they were knocked out in qualifying and only progressed to the finals on the strength of their world ranking after the Confederation of African Football decided to expand the tournament to 16 teams midway through the preliminary process.

While the first Women's Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon) semi-final was littered with chances and incident, the late game in the capital was a far tighter affair.

Morocco created little to reflect their dominance of the ball against an organised and disciplined Cameroon side who grew in confidence in the latter stages of the second half.

The Atlas Lionesses came close to an opener in the 14th minute when Sanaa Mssoudy diverted Hanane Ait El Haj's right-wing cross against the right-hand upright, and the forward also thrashed into the side-netting on the hour mark.

A flurry of late chances came at the end of regulation time, with Imane Saoud shooting straight at Bihina, Mssoudy heading wide and Michaela Abam firing over the Morocco bar.

Abam then had a shot blocked towards the end of the first period of extra time and Morocco defender Atiq headed over in the second half.

The match's key incident came right at the end of extra time when Morocco were presented with a glorious chance to win the tie following a video assistant referee (VAR) review, with Togolese official Vincentia Amedome deciding Nyadjou had caught Ouzraoui in the face with her arm.

Ait El Haj had converted from the spot in the quarter-final win over South Africa but substitute Tagnaout assumed responsibilities and the winger's tame left-footed effort was palmed away by Bihina.

There was more to come from the Cameroon keeper, who plays in her homeland for Benfica and had previously made a remarkable nine stops in her side's quarter-final upset against 10-time champions Nigeria.

Chapelle put her effort too close to Bihina but two stunning stops followed to deny Atiq and Ouzraoui.

Khadija Er-Rmichi had kept her side in the shootout by saving an effort from Grace Mendoua, but the Morocco keeper had little answer to Bihina's heroics.

A semi-final defeat comes as a big blow to Morocco, who have invested heavily in football in recent years and hired Spain's Women's World Cup winning manager Jorge Vilda in an attempt to claim a maiden continental crown.

The Atlas Lionesses were runners-up in 2022 and reached the final of the delayed 2024 Wafcon last July, but threw away a 2-0 half-time lead against Nigeria and were forced to settle for second place again.

Cameroon, meanwhile, return to the final for the first time since losing to Nigeria as tournament hosts in 2016.

The Indomitable Lionesses have lost three previous finals and coach Valentine Nguele, who only took charge in June, will need to nullify the threat of the Chawinga sisters Tabitha and Temwa when her side come up against Malawi on Sunday.

Whoever comes out on top, it will be a new name on the trophy.

On Thursday Ivory Coast take on Ghana (17:00 GMT) and Nigeria meet South Africa (20:00 GMT) in African play-offs for the chance to go into an inter-continental qualifier for the 2027 Fifa Women's World Cup.

title: 'I'd never watched the Olympics' - Evans on gymnastics fame
description: British gymnast Ruby Evans speaks to BBC Sport about how she copes with fame and followers ahead of the 2026 European Artistic Gymastics Championships.
fullText:
Ruby Evans did not appreciate the scale of what she was about to do back in the summer of 2024.

Competing at the Paris Olympics as a 17-year-old catapulted her into the spotlight.

Two years on - with a Commonwealth gold medal, 127,000 Instagram followers and almost two million likes on TikTok - the gymnast is of one of Britain's rising stars.

"I didn't actually think I'd get that many followers after the Olympics," she told BBC Sport.

"Because I was so young, I'd never really watched an Olympics. I didn't actually realise how many people watched the Olympics.

"I remember just opening my phone [after competing] and it wouldn't even turn on, there was just so much going on."

Success has required resilience. Never more so than at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

On the Sunday evening, Evans left the arena in tears after a disappointing sixth in the individual all-around competition.

On Tuesday she returned to earn Wales a historic gold in the floor final..

She said afterwards she'd turned her anger into motivation, with the proud Welsh gymnast claiming her "dragon was absolutely firing" for her gold medal-winning performance.

Despair to delight for Wales' golden girl Evans

'I feel amazing' - gymnast Evans on Olympic selection

Social media attention can bring a dark side.

Female athletes in a range of sports have complained about the abuse they get - from rugby to tennis players.

Evans is no stranger to negative comments - but she refuses to let it affect her.

"It doesn't matter who you are, you're going to get nasty comments," she said.

"But if they're not doing anything better and they can only comment on other people's lives, then you're already winning.

"I know some people will get offended by it and that's obviously OK. I just say never show the person that you're offended because they're going to keep doing it.

In a period of new faces in British gymnastics, 19-year-old Evans is well placed to become the next star of her sport.

At the Paris Olympics, she and her team-mates came agonisingly close to a medal, finishing fourth by 0.2 points in the women's team final.

She followed up her debut Olympics with a silver medal in the floor event at the 2025 World Championships.

After that gold in Glasgow, she is aiming for more success at this week's European Championships in Zagreb, Croatia - which will be live on the BBC from Saturday.

For someone who routinely sails through the air, her feet are firmly on the ground.

She says she is not driven by medals. Improving as a gymnast is her biggest motivation.

But asked if she's targeting gold at the LA 2028 Olympics, she smiles.

"Maybe," she adds. "If I'm good."

For individual success at an Olympics, she will need to showcase two vaults with different entries on to the vault.

So that is her current focus in training.

"Maybe if I get a second vault, I'd have quite a good chance," she added.

"But it's in gear two. It needs to get to gear five."

At the Europeans, Evans and her team are focusing on a strong performance in Sunday's women's team final as that will set them up for October's World Championships - and with it a chance of Olympic qualification.

As ever, there's likely to be a lot of attention on Evans - she's been showing she is someone worth keeping an eye on.

title: Jones turns to geese to inspire Japan
description: Before their second Test against Australia, Eddie Jones reveals an interesting method he uses to coach Japan - watching videos of geese fly in formation.
fullText:
Eddie Jones has revealed an interesting method he uses to coach his Japan side - watching videos of geese fly in formation.

Japan are facing Australia in a two-Test, home and away series this month, and Jones' side were beaten 35-32 by the Wallabies in Osaka last weekend.

The former England coach has made five changes for the second Test in Townsville, Australia on Saturday, including picking university student Yoshitaka Yazaki on the wing and giving Shunsuke Uenobo his first start at centre.

Jones said Japan's support play "wasn't as sharp as we would have liked" in the opening game, so he has turned to nature to get his point across.

"The reason we watch videos of geese is that the head of the flock is like the ball-carrier," the Australian said.

"The ball carrier is king, and then everyone else has got to follow after that.

"The geese fly hundreds, thousands of miles in formation and they follow the one goose in front, and it's the responsibility of the support players to respond to what the ball-carrier does."

Australia overcame an early red card for Miles Amatosero to defeat home side Japan and seal their first win under new head coach Les Kiss, who succeeded Joe Schmidt earlier this year.

With his geese videos in hand, Jones said Japan have "set ourselves the task of really taking it to Australia this week".

He added: "We're very disappointed to lose the last game, so the most important thing now is how we take on this game."

title: Can Sunderland defy the Premier League doubters again?
description: Sunderland were one of the stories of the 2025-26 Premier League season - but can they do it again this time around, with added European commitments?
fullText:
Sunderland were one of the stories of the 2025-26 Premier League season.

Promoted from the Championship through the play-offs in May 2025, the Black Cats marked their return to the top flight after an eight-year absence with a remarkable campaign.

Tipped for relegation by many, Sunderland ended the campaign in seventh to qualify for Europe for the first time since 1973.

So why - outside newly promoted teams Hull City, Coventry and Ipswich - are Sunderland once again among the bookmakers' favourites for the drop?

There are three main reasons their doubters can point to: their poor underlying numbers last season, the 'second-season syndrome' for promoted sides and a European campaign to contend with.

But are those reasons justified?

A youngster to watch at each Premier League club this season

Murtagh: 'Second season syndrome is lazy punditry'

While results and where you finish in the table are ultimately all that matter, Sunderland's underlying statistics from last season suggest repeating their success might not be so simple.

Expected goals (xG) tells us how well teams do the basics of creating lots of good chances and limiting their opponents to few low-quality ones, based on how hundreds of teams before them have scored or conceded from those opportunities.

Only relegated Burnley and Wolves had a lower xG difference than Regis le Bris' side last season, while West Ham - with the fourth-worst overall xG - were also relegated.

While Aston Villa and Sunderland made a mockery of xG by finishing much higher in the table, the majority of sides finished mostly in line with their underlying numbers, showing those two overachievers were more the exception that proves the rule.

Indeed, the three sides with the best xG difference finished in the top three in the same order, while - excluding Sunderland - the five sides with the worst made up the bottom five.

Only Man City and Aston Villa overperformed their xG numbers by more than the Black Cats, who scored three more goals and conceded six fewer than expected given the number and quality of shots taken.

So taking the season as a whole, it seems that Sunderland's performances weren't as impressive as their results. But one event significantly affected part of the Black Cats' season: the Africa Cup of Nations.

They were without six players - twice as many as any other side - during the tournament in December and January. While the club's performances had already declined after a strong start, they suffered even more when their squad was stretched.

But once all those players returned, Sunderland's underlying numbers improved throughout the rest of the season and they ended the campaign playing like a mid-table side.

With no Afcon this season, the Black Cats may not suffer such a drop in performance. If they continue the 2026-27 season as they finished the last then relegation should be only a remote possibility.

The belief that promoted sides that stayed up in their first season are often relegated in their second is a popular one, with the phrase 'second-season syndrome' regularly thrown about. But is it as common as people think?

Last season Sunderland and Leeds became the 53rd and 54th promoted sides to survive in the Premier League.

Of the previous 52, only 11 were relegated the following season (21%). The vast majority of promoted teams that stay up do not suffer from second-season syndrome.

However, there is precedent for a promoted side that had a first season as good as Sunderland's to be relegated in their second. In fact, the best promoted side in the 38-game era of the Premier League did just that.

George Burley's Ipswich ended the 2000-01 campaign fifth with 66 points - the highest finish and most points any promoted side has achieved in a 38-game season.

But with European football to contend with, they dropped 13 places and took 30 fewer points the next season as they were relegated in 18th place, with Sunderland the beneficiaries as they finished just one place above them.

Overall, four of the previous 20 promoted sides (20%) that finished in the top half in their first season suffered relegation in their second, with the most recent example being Sheffield United five years ago

The Black Cats were one of the sides that did not as they finished seventh under Peter Reid in 1999-2000 and followed up with another seventh-placed finish a year later (although that position did not bring European football back then).

Sunderland will be playing in Europe this season for the first time in 53 years, with at least eight games in the Europa League on top of their usual domestic commitments.

They are the 10th promoted side in Premier League history to qualify for Europe and just the fifth to do so through their league position, with the others qualifying via cup competitions or fair play.

Despite their squads arguably being the least-prepared to handle the extra fixtures, five of the previous nine teams achieved another top-half finish and just two were relegated - Ipswich in the early 2000s and Hull in the mid-2010s.

Hull were an unusual case as they only finished 16th with 37 points in 2013-14 but qualified for Europe by reaching the FA Cup final.

Their European campaign lasted just four games as they were knocked out in the Europa League qualifying rounds in August and were relegated with 35 points the following May.

But then there is that Ipswich side again.

When Inter Milan knocked them out in the Uefa Cup third round on 6 December 2001, Burley's side had won just one of their first 15 games in the Premier League.

While they did find some form after that - they were 12th with 30 points after 25 games - just one win in their final 13 matches led to relegation.

Sunderland will be hoping to follow the example of the most recent promoted side to qualify for Europe - Wolves in 2019.

Despite playing 17 games as they reached the Europa League quarter-finals in 2019-20, they still had enough in the tank to finish seventh in the league again.

There are definitely the ingredients for Sunderland to have a difficult second season, but given how well-run they have been in their recent rise from League One to Europe, many fans will have faith they will continue to thrive.

title: Only wins can stop curfew hokey-cokey for England's 'grown adults'
description: England have scrapped their midnight curfew seven months after introducing it. Now, only wins will repair the reputational damage they have sustained, says Stephan Shemilt.
fullText:
"We are grown men and we know how to behave," said Joe Root.

"As an international cricketer you are always representing the badge. We are a group of adults and we feel we can be treated like that."

Root did not say these words in 2026, but in his first stint as England captain in 2017.

It was the eve of an Ashes tour, one on which Root was without Ben Stokes because of the incident outside a Bristol nightclub.

The trip to Australia included the Jonny Bairstow-Cameron Bancroft 'headbutt' and Ben Duckett tipping a drink over James Anderson. The low point was Moeen Ali, a practising Muslim, being asked by a local journalist if he and the rest of the England players would be able to "stay out of the pub".

The midnight curfew imposed on that tour lasted more than four years until it was banished in 2022.

What is it about an away Ashes that drives Englishmen to drink? Trouble on the latest trip resulted in the return of the curfew in January yet, seven months later, Root's comeback as captain has seen the curfew, erm, put to bed.

Goodness knows what it says about the state of the England men's team that the subject of 'when grown men should go to bed' has been live for almost a decade.

You can be forgiven for struggling to keep up with England's hokey-cokey over the curfew in the past few months.

As a quick recap, rules that were introduced to the white-ball team in January were kept in place for the Test side at the beginning of the home summer.

After the first Test, captain Stokes and Gus Atkinson broke the curfew. Director of cricket Rob Key, fed up after a winter of misdemeanours, floated the idea of a total alcohol ban, while also admitting Atkinson didn't know the curfew was in place.

Head coach Brendon McCullum conceded there was some "ambiguity" around the regulations at the same time Stokes and Atkinson were cleared of any wrongdoing. Stokes came back, then retired.

Last month, England issued new guidelines to players, with the curfew still in place and advice for alcohol not to be drunk on the days immediately before, during, or immediately after a match.

England scrap midnight curfew after seven months

Then McCullum was sacked as Test coach. His last act in charge of both the Test and white-ball teams was to relax the drinking guidelines so England's T20 side could celebrate their series win against India.

Now the curfew is gone, under the instruction of Root and McCullum's replacement as Test coach - his great mate Stephen Fleming.

The England and Wales Cricket Board see Fleming as a grown-up, and he has made a grown-up move, one that also includes the curfew being lifted from a white-ball team still led by McCullum and Harry Brook.

McCullum is said to be supportive of players taking responsibility for their behaviour, which begs the question as to why he went along with the curfew in the first place.

Perhaps this is not a problem specific to this group of England players. Last week, Stokes rejected the idea that England have a drinking culture, instead suggesting the whole game has an unhealthy relationship with alcohol.

And that is not to say it is a crime every time a beer touches the lips of a cricketer.

In 2022, when England stunned New Zealand at Trent Bridge to give birth to the Bazball movement, the players celebrated on the dressing room balcony with a few drinks, then kicked on into the early hours and the Mega Munch takeaway in Nottingham.

After the Ashes of 2005, probably England's greatest series win, celebrations were led by a swaying Andrew Flintoff on an open-top bus through the streets of London.

Even this past winter, there's a decent chance Travis Head put away more than the England players. It's just that Head was scoring runs and Australia were winning.

Former cricketers will argue that any drinking taking place now is nothing worse than what was consumed in years gone by - Ian Botham, Allan Lamb, Phil Tufnell and the rest.

But perhaps that's exactly the point. Cricket has not moved with the times. You wouldn't catch famous Arsenal swillers Paul Merson and Tony Adams saying Declan Rice and Viktor Gyokeres could match them drink for drink.

It is also not fair to pin a drinking culture only on elite players. Cricket has a relationship with alcohol right down to the grassroots of the game.

I play league cricket (badly), mainly as an excuse to have a few beers.

On a Saturday, I couldn't really ask my partner to look after our two children just so I can go to the pub with 10 of my mates. Instead, I have to keep up the pretence of trying to score runs and catching the ball as a wicketkeeper. The cricket is a hindrance to getting to the bar.

Not that cricket will be too different to other amateur sports - back to the pub after Sunday league football, meeting in the bar at the tennis club, drinking games after a rugby match.

Has cricket kept up with the professional versions of those sports? Very much open to debate.

But these wider problems of the entire game are not an excuse for an England team who, frankly, would be given a pass for endless hours after midnight if they were winning.

Trouble is, they aren't, with only two victories in their past 10 Tests. The reputational damage that has been suffered over the past year will only be fixed by success on the field.

The first opportunity to start putting things right comes with three matches against Pakistan, beginning next week. After that, England's Test future is about as tough as it gets, with the major series coming away to world champions South Africa this winter, a home Ashes against Australia next summer, then five Tests in India in early 2028.

Does lifting the curfew enhance their chance of winning those series? Maybe treating the players like grown-ups off the field helps on it.

"If you want guys to take responsibility on the field, they've got to feel like they can be grown adults off it and make good, strong decisions off it," said Root on Wednesday.

Either way, England must decide their stance and stick to it. Much like constantly changing an opening pair does little for the team's output of runs, flip-flopping on rules around behaviour does not create a winning environment.

Curfew or no curfew, England can only rebuild on the field, not in the bar.

Win Tests, series and trophies, then they can go to bed as late as they please.

Rams star names 49ers nightmare he ‘hates’ facing
description: “There’s nobody that covers that much space,” Nacua said. “It’s scary. The middle of the field is terrible.”
fullText:
Puka Nacua has spent three NFL seasons tormenting defensive backs, but one San Francisco 49ers star apparently makes him reconsider the wisdom of crossing routes.

During an appearance on Logan Paul and Mike Majlak's "Impaulsive" podcast, the Los Angeles Rams receiver named Fred Warner the best defender he has faced — and said the middle of the field was akin to Warner's private haunted house.

"There's nobody that covers that much space," Nacua said. "It's scary. The middle of the field is terrible."

Nacua recalled running a route without receiving the ball, only to discover Warner waiting beside him with an explanation.

"He's like, 'I knew exactly where you're going,'" Nacua said. "Dude, I swear, when I started the play, you're on the left sideline, and now you're right here standing next to me."

Warner's response was not especially comforting: "That's just what I do."

Most linebackers pursue receivers. Warner apparently materializes beside them.

The four-time All-Pro's combination of speed, anticipation and coverage ability has made him the NFL's premier linebacker. Coaches and executives recently ranked Warner first at the position despite a broken and dislocated ankle limiting him to six games last season.

Nacua's fear comes with an important disclaimer: Warner has not exactly ruined his NFC West experience.

Across four games with Warner on the field, Nacua caught 34 of 43 targets for 357 yards and two touchdowns. Warner was credited as Nacua's primary defender on only two of those targets, allowing one seven-yard reception.

So Nacua has shredded the 49ers collectively while largely avoiding a direct appointment with the monster in the middle.

The rivalry also contains an awkward personal connection. Warner played at BYU with Nacua's older brother, Kai, leaving Puka caught between family familiarity and divisional obligation.

"Fred, I kind of hate you," Nacua recalled telling Warner. "We're supposed to not like each other, but I also enjoy watching you play."

That sounds less like trash talk and more like a frightened Yelp review: "Terrible experience. Five stars. Would reluctantly cross the middle again."

The two stars could renew their rivalry when the 49ers and Rams open the season in Melbourne. Warner is healthy and participating fully in training camp, while Nacua recently left a joint practice with minor groin soreness.

Nacua could also face NFL discipline stemming from offseason allegations, although the league has not announced a decision. His attorney has denied the claims against him.

If Nacua plays, San Francisco will again face one of the league's most productive receivers. He led the NFL with 129 receptions and 10 receiving touchdowns last season while finishing second with 1,715 yards.

Those numbers suggest Nacua is not afraid of much.

But when he enters Warner's territory, he apparently checks beneath the bed — and on both sidelines — before running his route.

title: Padres win 4-3 in 11 innings to sweep MLB-leading Brewers
description: Jackson Merrill hit a tying sacrifice fly in the 11th inning and Luis Campusano followed with a two-out single to bring in Sun-Mung Song from second base as the San Diego Padres beat the MLB-leading Milwaukee Brewers 4-3 on Wednesday for a three-game sweep.  The surging Padres have won five straight and 15 of 19 to move into the National League's second wild-card spot ahead of Arizona and Philadelphia.  Gary Sánchez doubled home the go-ahead run for Milwaukee off Adrian Morejon (9-2) in the top of the 11th.
fullText:
SAN DIEGO (AP) — Jackson Merrill hit a tying sacrifice fly in the 11th inning and Luis Campusano followed with a two-out single to bring in Sun-Mung Song from second base as the San Diego Padres beat the MLB-leading Milwaukee Brewers 4-3 on Wednesday for a three-game sweep.

The surging Padres have won five straight and 15 of 19 to move into the National League's second wild-card spot ahead of Arizona and Philadelphia.

Gary Sánchez doubled home the go-ahead run for Milwaukee off Adrian Morejon (9-2) in the top of the 11th.

Merrill tied it when his sac fly off Antonio Senzatela (9-4) brought in automatic runner Jake Cronenworth. Song, who pinch ran after Ty France was hit by a pitch, stole second before Campusano punched an opposite-field single to right. Luis Lara's throw home was high, allowing Song to slide in headfirst with the winning run.

The Padres tied the game at 2 with two outs in the eighth when Fernando Tatis Jr. raced around from second base to score on Cronenworth's infield single.

Cronenworth hit a bouncer to first baseman Jake Bauers, who flipped it to reliever Aaron Ashby but he was late covering first and Cronenworth beat him to the bag for an RBI single. Ashby turned toward home but didn't make a throw as Tatis sprinted in with the tying run.

Dustin May pitched brilliantly into the eighth for the Brewers. He allowed one run and four hits, struck out six and walked two. He gave up Xander Bogaerts' homer in the third.

Sánchez, who was with the Padres for part of the 2023 season, homered to left field against Robbie Ray in the second.

Brewers LHP Shane Drohan (6-4, 3.87 ERA) is scheduled to start opposite Dodgers RHP Roki Sasaki (5-5, 4.54) on Thursday in the opener of a four-game series in Los Angeles.

Padres RHP Michael King (7-8, 3.37 ERA) is set to start Friday in the opener of a three-game series at Cleveland, which counters with RHP Gavin Williams (11-6, 3.55).

title: Lions QB Josh Dobbs 'frustrated' with how Patriots handled release
description: Detroit Lions quarterback Josh Dobbs was not happy with how he was released by the New England Patriots.
fullText:
Detroit Lions quarterback Josh Dobbs is not happy with the way that the New England Patriots handled his release from the team.

The biggest gripe for the veteran signal-caller was the timing of the release.

It came nearly two weeks after free agency, putting Dobbs in a tough spot on the open market. He missed the initial rush of the free agency period, and an argument could be made that it might have limited his opportunities.

"It was a weird offseason because it was my first time not having OTAs and everything, and that was just by the nature of my situation in New England, with the timing. That was very frustrating, the way they handled that," Dobbs said, via Pro Football Talk's Michael David Smith.

Dobbs eventually agreed to a one-year deal with the Lions on Sunday.

Timing aside, the Patriots probably don't feel bad about their decision to move forward with Tommy DeVito as the top backup quarterback behind Drake Maye. DeVito has had an impressive training camp in his second year in Josh McDaniels' offense.

The Patriots also have a young prospect developing behind the scenes with rookie sixth-round pick Behren Morton.

As for Dobbs, he will now try to make up for lost time in Detroit, where Jared Goff is the starting quarterback and Luke Altmeyer is the young prospect in training.

title: WNBA condemns 'bad-faith' actors amid discussion of transgender athletes, online hate after task force meeting
description: "There are no immediate eligibility matters affecting the WNBA, and we strongly denounce the bad-faith efforts to use these topics to demean or marginalize others."
fullText:
The WNBA spoke out about the "bad-faith" actors who have been dominating the discussion surrounding transgender athletes and online hate after a task force meeting on Wednesday.

WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert, team presidents and general managers met Wednesday at a previously scheduled meeting and addressed both topics among others.

"Today's meeting covered a wide range of topics, including ongoing discussions on transgender athletes and the continued hate and vitriol directed at players online," the league said through a spokesperson. "We will continue to engage all league stakeholders in the coming weeks and months. We will approach these important conversations thoughtfully and in alignment with the values of our league.

"There are no immediate eligibility matters affecting the WNBA, and we strongly denounce the bad-faith efforts to use these topics to demean or marginalize others."

A statement from a WNBA spokesperson on today's task force meeting, including discussions on transgender athlete participation and the online discourse. pic.twitter.com/VVzRHbh7XO

There are no transgender players in the WNBA or preparing to enter the WNBA. The CBA also states that "only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA."

Despite those facts, transgender athletes have been a large topic of discussion around the league in recent weeks after Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham spoke out on the topic in an ESPN feature. She supported barring transgender athletes from women's sports, which led to anti-trans protests outside of Fever away games and an incident between a Seattle Storm minority owner and two Cunningham fans.

Naturally, the topic of transgender athletes in the WNBA has spread like wildfire on social media and elsewhere ever since. It's something that's been co-opted by more than one former men's professional basketball player, too. Many within the WNBA, including Minnesota Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve, have spoken out about the importance of inclusion. Reeve even wore a shirt that read, "Trans Kids Belong" during a game against the Fever.

"[The league will] always approach this topic thoughtfully, respectfully, and in alignment with the longstanding values of our league," Engelbert said in a memo to teams on Friday. "Second, our player eligibility rules, unlike the eligibility rules of some other leagues and governing bodies, are collectively bargained. Lastly, preserving the integrity of our game and ensuring fair competition will always remain among the league's highest priorities.

"We recognize that this is a complex and nuanced topic, and we will continue to have important conversations with all of you and the Players Association in the weeks and months ahead."

The players association also issued a statement last Friday condemning recent hate and abuse.

"We embrace justice equity, diversity, and inclusion," the WNBPA said. "Those are the values that unite this Union and allow it to protect women's sports while creating transformational change. Hate, abuse, and demonization of any person or group of people, including transgender people, only fuel fear, division, and harm. We will continue to have hard conversations. But we will not be used as political pawns."
