title: Five Hacks Every Garmin Cirqa User Should Know
description: Skip the $59.99 official arm band with a cheap DIY workaround.
fullText:
For Garmin fans who want 24/7 data, but don't want to wear their heavy-duty sports watch 24/7, the Garmin Cirqa ($199) is an exciting new alternative to Whoop, Fitbit Air, and other screenless smart bands. This is the company’s first screen-free smart band, built to track fitness and wellness features around the clock, without needing a subscription.

Because the Cirqa has no screen, you might default to only do what Garmin's automatic detection decides for it. But when it comes to making the most of the Cirqa from the moment you unbox, there are clever hacks worth knowing. Here are five tips of my favorites—some official, and some discovered by reviewers and the community in these early weeks since the device's launch.

This is one of the more underrated features on paper. In Garmin Connect, go to Garmin Devices > Health & Wellness > Broadcast Heart Rate, and turn on Device Control. Once that's enabled, you can hold the side button on the Cirqa itself for three seconds until the LED flashes yellow, and it'll start broadcasting your heart rate without needing to touch the app again.

The Cirqa can broadcast over ANT+ to essentially unlimited receiving devices at once, and simultaneously over Bluetooth Smart to up to three separate connections, which means you could realistically stream your live heart rate to a cycling computer, a gym treadmill display, and an app like Zwift all at the same time. For anyone who already owns a Cirqa and was about to buy a separate chest strap for gym equipment or a smart trainer setup, this alone can save the extra purchase.

The Cirqa has no display, so there's no obvious way to "check the time" on it. But if you like the feel of a ticking analog reminder, you can get close. In the Garmin Connect app, go to your device, then Notifications & Alerts, and look at the alert options tied to activity and movement. Turning on Move Alert (Garmin's inactivity reminder) gives you a light buzz once an hour during your active hours, functioning like an unofficial hourly chime (even though it's technically triggered by extended sitting rather than the clock itself). It won't be perfectly precise to the top of the hour every time, but in daily use it lands close enough, especially if you're someone who deliberately avoids glancing at a phone all day.

The same Notifications & Alerts menu is where the real wellness tracking happens. You can enable alerts for stress spikes, sleep score readiness, goal completion, and general movement, effectively turning the Cirqa into a mini coach for hydration breaks, stretch breaks, or a moment of mindfulness—all depending on how you choose to interpret the buzz.

For actual wake-ups, go to Alarms > Add Alarm in the app, set your time, and toggle on Smart Wake Alarm if you want it to try waking you during a lighter sleep stage within the 30 minutes before your set time, or Quiet Start if you'd rather it ramp up gradually instead of buzzing at full strength immediately. Worth knowing upfront: In my testing (and I'm not alone here), the Smart Wake Alarm has a reputation for being less "smart" than advertised. While I've never personally experienced it going off outside its intended window, all the "smart" alarm has ever done for me is worked like a plain fixed alarm regardless of your alleged sleep stage.

Since there's no screen, most people assume the only way to check the battery is to open Garmin Connect. There's actually a faster method built into the hardware itself, as long as you go in and set it up.

In the Garmin Connect app, go to your device settings and open Power Manager, then turn on the Battery Status option. Once that's enabled, double-tapping the physical sensor module triggers a single confirmation buzz, followed by the LED flashing a color that corresponds to your remaining charge:

Flashing green = Charging in process

Solid red = Critically low battery

Combined with the favorite activity and hold-for-broadcast button shortcuts, this reinforces the sense that the Cirqa's single button and LED light help set this smart band apart.

And on the activity side, remember to use the side button as your manual override for anything the automatic detection struggles with—which is a lot so far. And since the Cirqa has no built-in GPS chip, any distance, pace, or route data during an activity comes from your paired phone running the Garmin Connect app, so keep your phone nearby if you want a real map of your run or ride, not just heart rate and duration.

Garmin sells an upper-arm band separately for $59.99, so if you'd rather track from your bicep than your wrist, that's an option worth exploring—especially if you do activities where a wrist-worn band gets in the way. Plus, upper arm placement might improve your heart rate accuracy overall, since it gives the sensor better contact with a meatier part of the body with less wrist-movement noise.

If you want the upper-arm placement, but don't want to pay for Garmin's official accessory band, it might look like you have no options. The Cirqa pod uses narrow, non-standard 14mm spring pins, so it seems like it won't just clip into generic 20mm bands off the shelf.

A few users have shared this type of hack, and I think this video from @ChaseTheSummit explains it best. The workaround is to buy a small 14mm-to-20mm metal adapter (originally made for Casio G-Shock watches), available for $14.99 on Amazon. That adapter bridges the Cirqa's small pod to the much wider world of inexpensive, stretchy 20mm bicep bands. It's not going to match the fit or finish of Garmin's own accessory, but it's a clever money-saving option.

If you do try this DIY option, make sure you don't just yank the stock fabric band off the pod: Use a small pin pusher tool to compress the internal spring pins inward first, then remove it. Forcing it off without releasing the pins is a good way to damage the housing.

title: Everything Already Announced Ahead of Made by Google 2026
description: Google spilled the beans before its main event even kicked off.
fullText:
Made by Google 2026 officially starts at 6 p.m. ET on Wednesday, but you wouldn't know it from today's tech headlines. Some eight hours before the event was scheduled to begin, Google seemingly announced all of the new hardware and software features it plans to reveal during its main keynote. Unless the company is saving some secrets for the show, it appears all the actual news from Made by Google is already out there.

As such, we already know all about Google's new Pixel 11 lineup, including the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, and Pixel 11 Pro XL. We've seen the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, the Pixel Watch 5, and even the Pixel Tag, Google's first AirTag competitor. Plus, Google shared some details on new features coming to these devices, as well as existing Pixel products. While we still need to wait until this evening to actually watch the full event, here's everything the company announced ahead of Made by Google 2026.

At first glance, Google's Pixel 11 series doesn't look all that different from the Pixel 10 series. The company chose to carry over the Pixel's current design, which means the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, and Pixel 11 Pro XL all feature a large, oval camera bump on the back, and a small circular camera cutout on the front. However, Google says it reduced the Pixel 11's camera bar thickness by 40%, which it advertises makes for a "virtually bumpless" experience when using a "Made by Google" case.

The Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL are brighter this year: Google says the displays can reach up to 3,600 nits, with an upgraded anti-scratch coating that the company claims more than doubles scratch resistance compared to the Pixel 10 Pro. All things considered, Google says the 11 Pros are the most durable Pixels yet.

It turns out the storage rumors were true: Google is dropping the 128GB models this year. All three Pixel 11 phones start with 256GB of storage, which is great for keeping large files on-device, but not so great for your wallet. While the 256GB option costs as much as last year's 256GB Pixel 10 devices, Google effectively raised the cost of entry by eliminating the cheaper 128GB option. Now, the cheapest Pixel 11 starts at $899.

All three Pixel 11 devices come with the new Tensor G6 chip, which unsurprisingly brings upgrades over last year's Tensor G5. Google says this chip's CPU supports 25% faster web browsing and opens apps 15% quicker. The TPU handles 50% more compute, which means the G6 can process on-device AI functions 3.5 times faster than before, at 3.5 times the energy efficiency.

Perhaps Google's "funnest" feature this year is "HiLight," a new LED that lives in the camera bar. Google says you can rely on the light for alerts, so you can keep tabs on important updates while your phone is face down. For example, you can assign colors to different contacts, so you know who's calling without having to pick up your phone. Plus, the light can glow in specific patterns when you talk to Gemini to indicate whether the AI is listening, "thinking," or responding to you. However, as Marques Brownlee highlights, there isn't much else you can do with HiLight, which seems like a missed opportunity—especially when other Android manufacturers, like Nothing, offer a ton of customization with their LEDs. Google says it plans to add new capabilities in the future, like message notifications from favorite contacts, but we'll have to wait to see whether the company decides to take full advantage of this fun hardware feature.

Google's Pixel line has always been known for its cameras, and this year is likely no exception. Google says all three of its Pixel 11 phones come with major camera upgrades. The Pixel 11, for instance, has a 48MP main sensor that adds 56% more light sensitivity, and the 5x telephoto lens now supports 30x "Super Zoom," thanks to the Tensor G6 chip. The Pros get some unique updates of their own: Google says the main sensor on each is brand new this year, and the telephoto sensor is now bumped up to 48MP with 30% more light sensitivity. Portrait Mode now works at 5x, and "Pro Zoom" now works up to 120x. Google says the Pixel 11's low-light photography should also look better now, as Night Sight works 4.5 times faster.

The Pixel 11 comes in four colors: "Pistachio," "Hibiscus," "Frost," and "Obsidian." The Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL are available in "Canyon," "Fog," "Olive," and all-matte "Obsidian." They also come with faster charging, especially on the Pros. Those phones support Qi 2.2 charging at 25W, and you can get 15 hours of battery on the Pixel 11 Pro XL with just 15 minutes of wired charging—assuming you have the right setup.

Google also announced the successor to the Pixel 10 Pro Fold today, but like the Pixel 11 series, it's a bit of a "blink and you'll miss it" update. These phones are quite similar, though Google touts some slight design upgrades: The new foldable is nearly 10% lighter and 1mm thinner than before. It has the same IP68 water and dust resistance as before, but now, the new glass fiber composite materials make the Pixel 11 Pro Fold "nearly impossible to crack," or so says Google. The company claims the foldable is three times more durable than the previous iteration, with improved crease performance on the hinge.

Like the Pixel 11 series, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold's displays are brighter this year, also reaching 3,600 nits of peak brightness. The Fold also gets the HiLight LED, though nothing is different on the foldable's light. This phone also supports Qi2.2 at 25W, and you can get up to 50% charge in 30 minutes when using a 30W wired charger. Google says the foldable can reach up to 24 hours of battery life, so, theoretically, you should be able to make it through a full day without needing to top off.

The Fold also gets Google's newest Tensor G6 chip, this time with 16GB of RAM. Google says that powers its new "sign-to-text" feature, which it developed with the Deaf community. This feature lets you sign in Live Transcribe, which then translates your sign language into text. Google says the feature works with both one-handed and two-handed signing. This new Fold also gets a new 48MP main sensor, and the telephoto camera now supports up to 30x Super Zoom.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold comes in either Obsidian or Olive. The phone starts at $1,899.

Google also announced the fifth generation of its Pixel Watch line. The new watch comes with the Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated processor, with 50% more RAM and a 12% faster CPU than last year's Pixel Watch 4. Google says the Pixel Watch 5 is its most accurate GPS route tracking ever, with double the accuracy of previous models. The company claims its tracking accuracy beats the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro.

Google says the Pixel Watch 5 has 15% more accurate sleep stage detection than before, so your sleep tracking should be 

While not specific to Pixel Watch 5, Google also announced "Health Guardian," a suite of features that track changes in your health over time, including trends in insulin resistance, blood pressure, sleep breathing quality, and the aforementioned breathing emergency detection. You'll get a monthly summary in the Google Health app that points out any notable changes. This works with "qualified Pixel Watches" and Fitbit Air, though Google didn't note exactly which Pixel Watches work with these new features.

The Pixel Watch 5 has a 3,000-nit "domed" Actua 360 display with 11 new complication styles. Google also added two new watch faces, with additional generative watch face options. The watch can run for up to 30 hours off the charger (41mm) or 40 hours (45mm).

It comes in Fog, Olive, or Canyon (41mm only), and starts at $399 (41mm) and $429 (45mm). There's also a Stephen Curry Special Edition (45mm) that starts at $579.

As it turns out, the rumors were also right about the Pixel Tag: Yes, Google has been working on its own version of Apple's AirTag. Instead of working with Apple's Find My network, Pixel Tag uses Google's Find Hub network to achieve the same goals. Pixel Tag can connect to more than a billion Android devices across the world to update its location using end-to-end encrypted information.

Google says the Pixel Tag is IP67 water- and dust-resistant, with a built-in speaker for locating the device. It also has its own button you can press to ping your phone, something AirTags don't come with. Like AirTags, Pixel Tags last one year on a single battery, which you can replace yourself.

Setting up a Pixel Tag is identical to setting up an AirTag: You hold the device near your phone, and setup instructions appear on-screen. From there, you can choose to share a Pixel Tag with up to 10 people. When you need to find a Pixel Tag, you can use both Ultra-Wideband and Bluetooth Channel Sounding for precision finding, which provides turn-by-turn directions to locate your tracker.

You can use Left Behind alerts to know whether you forgot an item, and your phone will tell you whether an unknown Pixel Tag is following you. Like AirTags, you can pick up a Pixel Tag for $29 a pop, or $99 for a four-pack. The Pixel Tag launches Nov. 11.

While Google isn't releasing any new earbuds today, it is updating its existing models. Pixel Buds Pro 2 are getting Dynamic ANC, which adjusts noise cancellation when the buds shift in your ears. You will be able to ask Gemini to adjust audio controls, such as setting bass levels, and Pixel Watch will be able to pause your earbuds' audio when it detects you fall asleep. Live Translate will work in over 70 languages when tapping your Buds, and Pixel Buds Pro 2 now come in Olive. (The software features start rolling out in September.)

title: Here's How the Cameras on Google's New Pixel 11 Phones Compare to the iPhone
description: Google just dropped the specs on the new Pixel 11 cameras.
fullText:
Ahead of its annual Made by Google event in New York City, Google revealed the details of its upcoming line of Pixel 11 phones, including specs of their all-important cameras. Pixel 11 phones will come in three versions: the base Pixel 11, the Pixel 11 Pro, and the Pixel 11 Pro XL. The Pro and Pro XL cameras have the same features, while the base model sports a slightly scaled-down photographic system.

The standard Pixel 11's camera setup is a step up from the Pixel 10, but not a gigantic leap. The main improvement is the brighter main sensor; the lenses are close to last year's hardware. Here's how it breaks down:

Main: 48MP wide camera (rear) with a 1/1.56" sensor (larger than last year's model) to improve light input.

Ultrawide: 13MP, which is identical to the Pixel 10's ultrawide camera specs.

Telephoto: 10.8MP telephoto with 5X optical zoom and a 30x digital zoom. Also the same as the Pixel 10.

Front camera: 10.5MP, also identical to the Pixel 10.

Google is throwing the heavy hardware improvements into its pro-level phones, bumping up both the resolution and sensor sizes across almost every lens.

Main: 50MP wide camera, with a 1/1.3" sensor for improved light-gathering.

Ultrawide: 48MP ultrawide camera, a big leap from the 13MP ultrawide of the base model.

Telephoto: 48MP telephoto with 5X optical zoom and an "AI-powered" 120x Pro Zoom.

Front camera: The Pro's 42MP selfie camera is a big step up from the 10.5MP camera on the base Pixel 11.

With Apple's iPhones holding down over 50% of the U.S. smart phone market compared to Pixel's 3%, Google faces a real battle to win over buyers. Camera quality is a powerful weapon in its arsenal. Most consumers consider the camera an important choice when choosing between cell phones, and it's the most important feature for about half of younger users. Here's how Pixel 11's pro tier camera stacks up against the iPhone 17 Pro's best camera offerings.

Main sensor: The Pixel 11 Pro edges out Apple slightly with a 50MP lens compared to the iPhone 17 Pro's 48MP, but megapixels are more complex than just "more is better." Apple's main sensor is 1/1.28," which is slightly larger than the Pixel's 1/1.3" sensor, and sensor size is more important to low-light performance and dynamic range than raw pixels. So this one's closer to a wash than the megapixel numbers suggest.

Ultrawide: It's dead even. Both phones feature 48-megapixel ultrawide lenses.

Telephoto: When it comes to zooming, Google is slightly ahead, offering 5x zoom to Apple's 4x, but in terms of digital zoom, the Pixel 11 Pro's 120x zoom towers over Apple's 40x zoom—in a way. Google's "pro zoom" is built on generative AI, producing plausible details for things it can't see, leading to a realistic-looking photo. Apple's approach uses AI more modestly, focusing on stacking multiple exposures to reduce noise and fill in details. The end result: Apple's extreme zoom is more grainy and noisy, but also more real.

Front camera: The Pixel has a real advantage here with a 42MP sensor compared to Apple's 18MP selfie camera.

Both lines of smart phone cameras are roughly equal in terms of raw power. The main difference is largely a philosophical one. Apple might be losing the extreme magnification fight by capping its digital zoom to a relatively modest 40x, but it's also avoiding producing photos that are largely a product of artificial intelligence. If you want to push the boundaries of what a lens can capture with the help of generative AI, and you're not overly concerned about verisimilitude, the Pixel is the choice. If you want to keep it real (well, real-ish, anyway) the iPhone is the choice.

title: Six New Features Coming to the Pixel Watch 5
description: Google's newest Pixel Watch comes with some exclusive features and changes.
fullText:
At first glance, you might think Google's new Pixel Watch 5 was actually the Pixel Watch 4. That's because it has the same "Actua 360 display" at an identical 320 PPI with up to 3,000 nits of brightness. And, just like the Pixel Watch 4, you can get the Pixel Watch 5 in either 41mm or 45mm models. If not for the new colors, you might think this year's watch is just like last year's watch.

It doesn't help that many of the newest software features that Google announced along with the Pixel Watch 5 are compatible with older watches, too. Things like "Health Guardian," which tracks trends in insulin resistance, blood pressure, and sleep breathing, will be available on Pixel Watch 4 when they launch, just as they will be on Pixel Watch 5. But while the Pixel Watch 5 is a small update to the Pixel Watch 4, it is an update: There are six new features exclusive to the watch that you won't find on older models.

The Pixel Watch 4 runs the Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 chip; the Pixel Watch 5 runs the Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated chip. That might not sound like a big difference, and, indeed, we don't have benchmarks at this time to say just how much faster the Pixel Watch 5 is than its predecessor.

However, according to Google, the Pixel 5's "Accelerated" chip is powering on-device AI features faster than before. That includes Google's "Raise to Talk" feature, which lets you interact with Gemini by raising your wrist. The company says these features on Pixel Watch 5 now process "instantly with low latency," even when you aren't connected to the internet.

The chip also powers Gemini Intelligence Proactive Suggestions (Google previously called this Magic Cue). These are new suggestions that automatically appear based on the context of what you're doing: If someone asks you for your flight info, Gemini can use your Pixel Watch 5's chip to dig through your apps to surface that info by presenting it as an option to share with a tap. Google says the Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated chip has 50% more RAM than the previous generation, as well as a 12% CPU boost, which makes the whole chip 20% faster overall.

Google has some bold claims for the Pixel Watch 5. Not only does the company claim that its newest watch has the most accurate GPS route tracking of any Pixel Watch (the company says it has double the accuracy of previous generations in the "toughest environments"), Google says its more accurate than Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 Pro. We'll have to see how true those claims are when reviewers put the watch to the test.

To make these leaps in GPS route tracking, Google says it tapped into Google Maps to "trace satellite ray paths through 3D building models." The company also explains how Pixel Watch 5 can connect to weather reference stations around the globe in real time to adjust for local atmospheric conditions. Google claims all these steps improve route precision.

While Pixel Watch 4 shares many of the new health features Google is rolling out in coming months, the Pixel Watch 5 does win in certain categories. Google says the newest watch has 15% more accurate sleep stage detection, which should improve sleep tracking overall. In addition, your bedtime automation on the Pixel Watch 5 can pause audiobooks automatically when you fall asleep, and there's now a dedicated bedtime watch face.

Google says Pixel Watch 5 comes with two new "stunning" watch faces, as well as 11 new "glanceable" complication styles. The company didn't highlight what those looked like in their press releases, but 9to5Google has images of the faces (Weave and Chronograph). You can also use AI to generate new watch faces if the available options aren't to your liking.

Google says the Watch 5 has three new color options, though only two are available in both sizes. Those include Fog, Olive, and Canyon, though the latter is a 41mm exclusive. If you're set on the 45mm model, you could instead choose the Stephen Curry Special Edition, as that model isn't available in 41mm.

One health feature exclusive to Pixel Watch 5 is "breathing emergency detection." Google says the Pixel Watch 5 can use on-device AI to read its PPG, accelerometer, and barometer sensors all at once, in an effort to detect if you stop breathing. That could be from drug toxicity accidents, pneumonia, or choking. The company says if your watch detects a breathing emergency and you can't respond, it will reach out to emergency services on your behalf, even sharing your live location. This feature is launching in Europe first.

title: You Can Still Get a Samsung Galaxy Z Phone With a $350 Amazon Gift Card
description: The Galaxy Z Flip8, Galaxy Z Fold8, and Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra phones are all up for grabs with Amazon gift cards and trade-in credits.
fullText:
Samsung announced five new products during its Galaxy Unpacked event last month. Three of those are the new flagship smartphones: the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Z Flip 8. Amazon had pre-order deals that were supposed to last until their launch, but the deal is still active after their release. We don't know for how long, so if you're interested, get it before it's gone. You can get an Amazon gift card up to $350, while Samsung is offering a max of $230 in Samsung credits. And if you're looking to switch to T-Mobile, you can get a Galaxy Z Fold 8 on them. You can read more details on that deal here.

If you were expecting a shiny new toy from the Z Flip 8, you might be disappointed—it's not that different from the Z Flip 7. It has a 4.1-inch outer display and a 6.9-inch inner display, 12GB of RAM, and similar cameras to the Z Flip 7, including a 50MP Wide, 12MP Ultra Wide, and 10X Digital Zoom. Upgrades over the previous model include peak brightness that's 1000 nits brighter, now reaching 2600 nits; there is a new 2x optical zoom; and the processor upgrades the SoC from the Exynos 2500.

As Lifehacker Senior Tech Editor Jake Peterson says, the Z Fold 8 is not the upgraded version of the Z Fold 7: It's a brand new device, which might appeal to users who want a phablet that takes up a little less space in their pocket. You can expect a 5.5-inch outer display, a 7.6-inch inner display, three rear cameras (50MP Wide, 50MP Ultra Wide, and 2x Optical Zoom), and the same Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip as the rest of the "Z 8" line.

The flagship foldable Samsung phone for 2026 is the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. It has the biggest and best cameras (200MP Wide, 50MP Ultra Wide, and 10MP Tele), the largest displays (6.5-inch outer display, 8-inch inner display), and the biggest battery (5,000 mAh).

title: Four Features Coming to Every New Pixel 11 Device
description: The Pixel 11 series is a modest update, but the devices do come with notable features.
fullText:
Hours before its big Made by Google event, Google officially unveiled the Pixel 11 series. The new line won't come as a surprise to anyone who follows Google tech: There's the new Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, as well as the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—for anyone who can get past the $1,899 starting price.

Each of these devices stands out in its own way: The Pixel 11 Pro XL is larger than the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro, while the Pixel 11 Pro Fold can open up to reveal one large inner display. Google has set up this series to allow customers to pick the phone that best aligns with their needs, but there are also features you get no matter which phone you go with. In fact, there seem to be four such upgrades each Pixel 11 device comes with. If you're looking for preorder deals, check out our guide here.

Google's Pixel line might be best known for its cameras. As such, it only makes sense that the Pixel 11 series would ship with upgraded shooters. The Pixel 11 now has a 48MP main camera that Google says is 56% more sensitive to light. Plus, the 5x telephoto lens now supports Google's 30x "Super Zoom."

The Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL also get brand new sensors on the main cameras, while the telephoto camera gets bumped up to 48MP. Google says its new image sensor is 30% more light-sensitive than before. The Pros also support Portrait Mode at 5x zoom, and "Pro Zoom" at 120x. And when shooting in low-light conditions, Night Sight is now 4.5x faster than it was on Pixel 10 Pro. Finally, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold also comes with a new 48MP main camera that supports 30x Super Zoom.

No matter which Pixel 11 device you choose, Google says you get upgraded charging over last year's Pixel 10. The Pixel 11 gets the fewest upgrades here, however: Google says it has the "fastest charging yet," using PixelSnap built-in, but that appears to be it.

All three "Pro" Pixel 11 devices, however, now support Qi 2.2, a faster wireless charging standard. If you use a 25W charger, you should notice quicker speeds when wirelessly charging. The Pixel 11 Pro XL might be the phone to get if charging speeds are your thing, however. With a 45W USB-C charger, Google says you can get 15 hours of use with 15 minutes of charging.

As with most smartphone upgrades, this year's series gets Google's latest chip: the Tensor G6. The company says Tensor G6 is the "fastest, most powerful" Google chip yet, and features a CPU that supports 25% faster web browsing and 15% faster app launches. The company claims the new chip can power on-device AI tasks 3.5x faster than Tensor G5, while at the same time being 3.5x more efficient than before. That should help power all of the AI features Google continues to push.

Say goodbye to 128GB of storage. Starting with the Pixel 11 series, all of Google's phones now start at 256GB. That news isn't as good as it sounds, though: While your base model Pixel 11 will have double the storage of a base model Pixel 10, Google still charges the same for 256GB as it did last year. That means the company effectively raised the entry price for each Pixel 11 device.

A previous version of this article reported that Pixel 11 shipped with HiLight, but that feature is only available on Pixel 11 Pro devices.

title: An overnight Ukrainian blitz damages Russia's Black Sea naval stronghold, Zelenskyy says
description: Ukrainian anti-ship missiles and drones blitzed a major Russian naval base on the Black Sea coast in a “unique” nighttime operation, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday.  Cutting-ed...
fullText:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian anti-ship missiles and drones blitzed a major Russian naval base on the Black Sea coast in a "unique" nighttime operation, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday.

Cutting-edge drones developed by Kyiv since Moscow's full-scale invasion over four years ago have repeatedly targeted Russian ships in the Black Sea, including warships and oil tankers.

Ukraine's air and sea drones have succeeded in limiting the movements of Russia's once-dominant Black Sea navy, Kyiv officials say, in one of the country's biggest accomplishments of the war.

But Ukrainian officials believe Russian President Vladimir Putin is bent on pressing ahead with the war, despite his bigger army's slow and costly progress on the battlefield and U.S. diplomatic efforts to find a settlement.

Putin is planning "an additional rapid mobilization of several hundred thousand Russians by the end of the year," Zelenskyy said Tuesday night on social media, citing Ukrainian intelligence reports.

Those reports have said recently that Russia is expanding production of ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, both of which are hard for Ukrainian air defenses to counter.

Ukraine also is trying to scale up its weapons manufacturing through agreements with partner countries.

Neither Putin nor other senior Russian officials have hinted at a possible major call-up of forces to fight in Ukraine. Some officials have accused Kyiv of trying to rattle the Russian public with talk of a mobilization.

Russian lawmaker Andrei Gurulyov brushed off reports of a possible autumn mobilization. "It is the enemy deliberately spreading rumors about mobilization in order to destabilize the situation inside Russia," he was quoted as saying by pro-Kremlin online outlet Tsargrad in comments published Monday.

After the widely unpopular partial mobilization of some 300,000 men four years ago, Russia has relied on volunteers attracted by relatively high pay. However, the decree declaring the partial mobilization that Putin signed in September 2022 is open-ended, allowing authorities to resume it if needed.

The Ukrainian military "carried out a unique operation targeting the naval base in Novorossiysk — the last major stronghold of the Russian fleet in the Black Sea," Zelenskyy said in a social media post Wednesday. The attack struck air defenses, piers and other port infrastructure, he added.

Russia relocated most of its naval ships to Novorossiysk after Ukrainian strikes on the main Black Sea base at Sevastopol on the Crimean Peninsula earlier in the war.

Hundreds of Ukrainian drones attacked Novorossiysk, Anapa and Gelendzhik and the Temryuk district of the Krasnodar region overnight, said Gov. Veniamin Kondratyev.

An 8-year-old child was one of three people killed in the attack on the region, Kondratyev said. He added that 24 others in the region were wounded. Dozens of residential buildings were damaged, Kondratyev said, and debris from downed drones fell on the grounds of four industrial plants.

The strikes damaged two of Novorossiysk's three grain terminals, with one of them halting operations, the Russian business daily Vedomosti reported.

Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed more than 500 Ukrainian drones.

Novorossiysk also is home to the Grushovaya oil terminal, one of the largest international hubs in southern Russia for petroleum products. No reports indicated it had been hit.

In February, the U.S. State Department expressed its displeasure about Ukraine's attacks on Novorossiysk, saying they affected U.S. oil interests in ⁠Kazakhstan.

The Caspian Pipeline Consortium operates a pipeline from the Caspian coast in northwestern Kazakhstan to Novorossiysk. The pipeline handles much of the crude exports from three major Kazakh fields in which major U.S. energy companies, Chevron and ExxonMobil, have stakes.

With the militaries of European countries boarding and detaining sanctioned Russian oil tankers at sea, hurting the country's trade and heaping economic pressure on Moscow, Putin on Wednesday threatened retaliation for what he termed "piracy."

Speaking on a visit to a Russian warship taking part in a naval exercise in the Pacific, Putin said Western countries are breaking international maritime law by seizing ships they say are part of Moscow's " shadow fleet " of sanctions-dodging merchant vessels.

"It's nothing but piracy and robbery," Putin said. "If this is done, we will be forced to respond in kind."

On the Crimean Peninsula, which was illegally annexed by Moscow in 2014, air defenses downed 115 Ukrainian drones over Sevastopol overnight, said Mikhail Razvozhayev, the city's Russian-installed head. He added that 10 apartment buildings and 25 private houses were damaged.

Ukraine's air force said Russia fired 138 long-range drones as well as an unspecified number of missiles during the night, with damage recorded at 16 locations.

In the Kherson region of southern Ukraine, a large-scale Russian drone attack overnight killed two people and wounded two others, said regional head Oleksandr Prokudin.

The attacks also destroyed a shopping mall in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, according to authorities.

Missiles and long-range drones hit fuel reservoirs and infrastructure used for unloading and storing military cargo in the port of Chornomorsk in Ukraine's Odesa region, Russia's Defense Ministry said.

A bulk cargo vessel carrying military equipment and a tanker loaded with oil for the Ukrainian armed forces also were hit in Odesa, it said.

Follow the AP's coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Nearly a dozen firms are already paying up to $100,000 per month for early access Trump’s Truth Social posts
description: The release of Truth API has raised concerns about insider trading among economists and legal experts.
fullText:
More Wall Street customers are signing up for a Trump Media & Technology Group service that allows earlier access to new Truth Social posts, a feature some economists are calling a form of insider trading.

Trump Media, founded by President Donald Trump in 2021, announced more than 10 customers have signed up for Truth API, or Application Programming Interface, a service that began earlier this month that gives Wall Street traders access to Truth Social posts from top users, including Trump, milliseconds before being published for the platform's broader audience. Customers are charged between $60,000 and $100,000 per month for the service.

Interim CEO Kevin McGurn said during the company's earnings presentation on Monday  most Truth API customers are high-frequency trading firms, but it is in talks to sell the product to hyperscalers, large news organizations, and large-language model developers, as well as expand the tool for retail trading. McGurn said the product was in "early innings," but the company was "strongly encouraged" by early progress.

"We believe this can grow into a meaningful, durable contributor," McGurn said, "but it is just one piece of a broader media technology strategy that also includes advertising, subscriptions, and our digital asset treasury."

The rollout of Truth API coincides with the company reporting a loss of $238 million between April and June, more than 10 times the magnitude of the quarterly losses a year ago, as it branched out beyond media, such as cryptocurrencies. The Truth API feature is part of the company's turnaround plan focusing on social media.

The product underscores Trump's ability to move markets by announcing major policy changes on the platform. In April, Trump posted he would pause planned strikes on Iranian infrastructures following threats contingent upon reopening the Strait of Hormuz, leading to a $1.5 trillion stock market rally.

But the product, as well as Trump's continued stake in the company, has garnered several ethical concerns. Trump owns about 41% of company shares for Trump Media, leaving him to benefit from the new revenue stream of Truth API subscribers, which at just 10 users, could drive up to $1 million in monthly revenue, or $12 million annually. The new feature, according to experts, effectively allows Trump to financially gain from his own official statements.

"I'll be blunt," Gian Luca Clementi, an economics professor at NYU Stern School of Business, told Fortune. "This is insider trading by definition."

title: Singapore and S Korea pull Trader Joe's seasoning over poppy seeds
description: Trader Joe's Everything But the Bagel seasoning contains poppy seeds which are banned in both countries.
fullText:
Singapore and South Korea have pulled Trader Joe's Everything But the Bagel seasoning from e-commerce platforms because it contains poppy seeds.

While they do not naturally contain opiates, poppy seeds are banned in both countries because they can get contaminated with opiates by fluid in the poppy plant during harvesting.

More than 20 online listings of the popular seasoning have been removed, Singapore's Central Narcotics Bureau said on Wednesday.

Last week, Seoul authorities said the seasoning tested positive for morphine and codeine, which are opiates found in the plant's sap.

Apart from poppy seeds, the product also contains sesame seeds, sea salt, minced garlic and minced onion. It was released by American grocery chain Trader Joe's in 2017.

Authorities in Singapore have urged anyone who has bottles of the seasoning to dispose of them.

"Singapore adopts a strict policy of zero tolerance towards controlled drugs," the narcotics bureau said, according to a CNA report.

"The possession, consumption, importation, exportation, manufacturing and trafficking of any controlled drug, even in trace amounts, is an offence under the Misuse of Drugs Act," it said.

In South Korea, investigators say some people brought the seasoning back home as souvenirs from their overseas trips before listing it for resale.

Some did so without realising it contained controlled substances, while others did so knowingly, according to a report by The Korea Herald.

"Even if a product is legally sold overseas, it may be classified as a narcotic substance or a prohibited import in Korea, so particular caution is required," a police official said.

title: More history made at Croke Park as Man Utd beat Leeds
description: Less than a month after Mayo's historic win in the All-Ireland final at Croke Park, a stadium that is famous for sliotars and the Sam Maguire turned its attention to one of the oldest rivalries in English football.
fullText:
Less than a month after Mayo's historic win in the All-Ireland final at Croke Park, a stadium that is famous for sliotars and the Sam Maguire played host to one of the oldest rivalries in English football on Wednesday night.

With a new Premier League season approaching, the friendly gave fans of both Manchester United and Leeds United an opportunity to see their teams in action, plus witness the spectacle of a solar eclipse.

The match marked another big night for Croke Park in what has been a summer to remember.

Manchester United ran out 5-4 winners in a penalty shootout after the teams played out a 1-1 draw in front of the raucous 82,300-capacity crowd in Dublin.

Both sets of clubs have plenty of Irish connections so their fourth friendly in eight years being in Ireland was fitting.

The likes of Belfast's George Best helped pave the way for a new generation of Manchester United fans, while former right back Gary Kelly's shirts were prominent amongst the Leeds support.

The sunny Dublin streets were filled with anticipation and plenty of excitement as kick-off approached with lots of 'if we sign one more striker then this will be a good season' talk filling the walkway to Croke.

This match was highly anticipated and was the third time that Association football has been played after the Gaelic Athletic Association's Rule 42 which prevented 'foreign' sports being played in the stadium was amended.

The game also ended a nine-year wait for a football match at Croke Park and was the first time that two English soccer teams had played there, but after the success of this night, it may not be the last.

Once the match got under way, it was the Manchester United fans who had more to cheer about in the opening encounters after Joshua Zirkzee's first-time strike gave them the lead after just 16 minutes.

Known for its electric atmosphere, the sold-out Croke crowd did not disappoint, and Leeds levelled the match against the run of play thanks to the unmarked Brenden Aaronson.

However, the Dublin fans were not treated to a classic with chances at a premium in the second half.

The lack of goalscoring opportunities did not dampen their spirits though, with Man Utd captain Bruno Fernandes and summer signing Youri Tielemans' introductions being met with enthusiastic cheers.

It was also a memorable night for substitute stopper Dermot Mee, who has played for Northern Ireland at underage level and played a key part in the victory after being introduced as a second-half substitute.

After months of suspense-filled finals, this friendly was decided on penalties in front of Hill 16.

The famous stand has seen every All-Ireland final, Dublin summers and some great Gaelic games.

Known for holding over 13,000 supporters and being the location of many winning celebrations, the stand was a sea of colour from the Leeds supporters.

The regular attendees at Croke Park may have not been used to the club colours, new goalposts and different pitch markings, but the celebrations after Noussair Mazraoui's winning penalty mirrored the noise at the full-time whistle of many finals before.

Just as Jack Coyne lifted the Sam Maguire to end Mayo's years of heartbreak, Fernandes collected the trophy as choruses of 'glory, glory Man United' rang around Croke Park and as supporters spilled onto the streets of Dublin.

title: More than 24,000 cyclosporiasis infections reported as new cases appear to slow: CDC
description: Cyclosporiasis is behind an outbreak linked to shredded iceberg lettuce.
fullText:
Cases of cyclosporiasis have topped 24,000, according to the most recent data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

There are at least 13,895 laboratory-confirmed cases of cyclosporiasis, including 740 hospitalizations, the data shows.

The agency is also aware of at least 10,455 additional cases that have not yet been laboratory confirmed.

The rate of increase appears to have slowed, with only about 2,000 more cases recorded over the last week. The previous week saw more than 22,000 cases recorded, a jump of over 10,000 from the week prior.

What to know about the latest food outbreaks in the US linked to lettuce, jalapeños

The CDC data, which was released on Tuesday, shows the ages of those who have fallen ill range between 1 and 98 years old.

There is a six-week reporting lag between when people feel sick and case reporting to the CDC, indicating that numbers will likely continue to rise.

It comes amid an outbreak now linked to now-recalled iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms that has spread to at least 15 states.

A total of 6,358 illnesses has now been reported across those states amid the outbreak, and at least 278 hospitalizations.

"The true number of sick people in this multistate outbreak is likely higher than the number reported, and the outbreak may not be limited to the states with known illnesses," a notice from the Food and Drug Administration investigation reads.

Michigan health officials say people can resume regular lettuce-eating habits as new cases of cyclosporiasis slow

Two deaths have been reported in Michigan in the cyclosporiasis outbreak, both individuals with significant underlying health conditions, health officials in the state said this week.

Originally, illnesses were isolated to shredded lettuce served at Taco Bell in nine states. However, health officials have found that the lettuce was also distributed to food services, retail stores and restaurants.

The lettuce was sourced in central Mexico and distributed by Taylor Farms. Last month, Taylor Farms issued a voluntary recall of all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico.

title: Airports Are ICE's Latest Target, Raising 4th Amendment Concerns From Airlines
description: An apparent surge of ICE arrests in airport terminals has created viral videos and questions over ICE's authority to board planes without judicial warrants.
fullText:
Federal immigration officers have dramatically stepped up the number of arrests inside airport terminals, leading to viral videos, criticism from immigrant rights groups, and pushback from U.S. airlines and airline employee groups.

The New York Times reported on July 28 that the Trump administration was targeting foreign nationals with expired visas as they traveled through airports. The story followed videos showing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents tackling a Ukrainian woman at San Francisco International Airport and arresting an Ecuadorian au pair in Denver, whose lawyer said she filed a pending application allowing her to stay in the country. In another video, ICE agents attempted to arrest a Vietnamese man at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas on July 13, but retreated as bystanders began to arrive and film the scene, leaving the man with a pair of handcuffs hanging off one of his wrists. A University of Maryland "teacher of the year" was detained on July 21, and a researcher for Baltimore's Johns Hopkins University was detained on July 28 by federal immigration officers while boarding a domestic flight.

Although the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) told news outlets that arrestees were in the country illegally, many of the reported cases of airport arrests appear to involve immigrants whose visas had expired but who were awaiting official adjudication of applications to change their status.

Immigrant rights groups believe the escalation is an attempt to meet the White House's steep daily quota for immigration arrests, which last month reached their highest level since President Donald Trump returned to office. The Trump administration's mass deportation campaign has not only targeted immigrants who are in the country illegally, but has attempted to end or raise the requirements for all possible legal and temporary means of immigration for millions of foreigners who have or are attempting to migrate to the country—from legal asylum to the right to a bond hearing in detention to birthright citizenship, even marriage.

"We think it's because ICE is pursuing detention quotas with regard to underlying eligibility for relief, applications for relief, and also because many of those people are already in the system," Kelly Rojas, a co-director at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, told CBS News. They "are easy targets for ICE."

As Felipe De La Hoz wrote in The New Republic, it's in fact common for immigrants on temporary visas to apply for a change in status and be explicitly instructed by the government to remain in the country while their application is pending. Although their visa is technically expired, the federal government typically considers this an authorized stay, and if the immigrant leaves the country, it's considered an abandonment of their petition.

"There are many versions of this circumstance," De La Hoz writes. "There are people who might be in affirmative asylum processes who have overstayed tourist visas. There might be those who had a status which the government subsequently attempted to terminate who are exercising their right to contest that termination. There are people who might have conditional green cards and are petitioning to remove those conditions (a situation that arises out of certain marriages), during which time the green card expires. What all these people have in common is that they are following the law—and they are in the country lawfully."

The apparent policy shift is causing headaches for U.S. airlines and airline employees. The Wall Street Journal reported last week that airline-industry representatives met with staffers from the DHS seeking clarity on whether ICE officers can use administrative warrants to board airplanes and make arrests.

The Journal also reported that the Association of Flight Attendants wrote to airlines in March expressing concern about immigration enforcement at airports.

"The actions that federal enforcement authorities have taken in our workplaces have raised glaring workplace, safety and legal concerns for flight attendants," Sara Nelson, international president of the union, wrote in the letter.

According to the Journal, Nelson cited reports of ICE agents gaining access to jet bridges without authorization, including one instance in which an agent in Minneapolis boarded a flight "in order to interrogate and threaten removal of a person who criticized their presence in the airport."

Trump administration officials repeatedly claimed earlier this year that ICE agents could rely on administrative warrants to enter private residences, not judicial warrants signed by Article III judges. However, the administration walked its rhetoric back under fierce bipartisan criticism. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said during his March confirmation hearings that "a judicial warrant will be used to go into houses, into places of business, unless [agents] are pursuing someone that enters in that place."

As Reason's Autumn Billings wrote, Mullin's statement left quite a lot of wiggle room for immigration officers.

"Given the Trump administration's comfort skirting constitutional and legal lines in the name of mass deportations, however, it's not outside the realm of possibility that Mullin's vague carveout for pursuit could open the door for future abuses by immigration officers," Billings wrote.

Apparently, that door is a jetbridge.

The post Airports Are ICE's Latest Target, Raising 4th Amendment Concerns From Airlines appeared first on Reason.com.

Russia is helping China close gap with US forces amid Taiwan tensions, warns longtime military leader
description: Retired Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery warns Russia is giving China submarine quieting technology that could erode a key U.S. Navy undersea advantage.
fullText:
Sound alarms are blaring over an escalating partnership between Russia and China to subvert the U.S. military amid rising hostility between the world powers.

Retired Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery tells Fox News Digital that Moscow may be providing Beijing with technology to make its submarines harder for the U.S. Navy to detect, potentially eroding a key military advantage in the tensions over Taiwan.

"Russia is giving incredibly important technology to China. They're allegedly giving them submarine quieting technology," Montgomery, co-author of the new book "Axis of Aggressors," told Fox News Digital.

Three Key Reasons Why America Cannot Afford To Lose Taiwan To Communist China

Montgomery said Russian forces are providing the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) with submarine-quieting technology, an area where China has long sought to improve its capabilities. Such a transfer, he warned, could weaken a critical U.S. advantage in undersea warfare — a gap that has long favored American forces.

"Any weakening of our asymmetric advantage in undersea warfare is a big deal," he cautioned.

The Navy says its submarine force relies on technological superiority and stealth to maintain its undersea advantage, while China has continued to face weaknesses in submarine propulsion and quieting even as it rapidly modernizes its fleet.

Quieting technology reduces a submarine's acoustic signature, making it harder to detect and track. Russian assistance in that area could help Beijing narrow the gap, complicating the U.S. Navy's ability to find Chinese submarines in a potential future conflict over Taiwan's independence from the CCP.

The Chinese Embassy did not directly address whether Beijing has received Russian submarine-quieting technology when reached by Fox News Digital.

"Military cooperation between China and Russia consistently adheres to the principles of non-alliance, non-confrontation, and non-targeting of third parties, playing a significant role in safeguarding the sovereignty and security of both nations and maintaining international and regional peace and stability," the embassy said in a statement. "We hope that relevant parties will view China-Russia military cooperation objectively and rationally, and stop groundless speculation."

The embassy said Taiwan is China's internal affair and urged the U.S. to safeguard stability in the bilateral relationship and across the Taiwan Strait.

Montgomery's warning echoes concerns raised by Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, who told the Senate Armed Services Committee in April 2025 that China was receiving "potentially submarine quieting help" from Russia.

Us Falls Behind In Hypersonic Race As China, Russia Gain Edge

Paparo said China's backing of Russia's war effort — including machine tools and legacy chips — was part of a broader exchange in which Moscow was returning assistance in military areas where it holds particular strengths.

The exchange reflects a deepening relationship in which Russia and China are increasingly providing capabilities the other lacks, Montgomery said.

"This transactional relationship is putting the United States and its most important allies and partners at risk," he said.

Paparo sounded a similar warning in November 2024, saying he expected Russia to provide China submarine technology that could help close America's undersea advantage. He described the relationship between Moscow and Beijing as a "transactional symbiosis."

China, meanwhile, has helped Russia rebuild its defense industrial base during the war in Ukraine. Paparo told senators Beijing provided 70% of the machine tools and 90% of the legacy chips that enabled Moscow to rebuild its war machine.

Montgomery said China's support extends beyond those supplies.

"And then China has backstopped the whole thing," Montgomery said, pointing to increased Chinese foreign direct investment and trade with Russia as well as components used in Moscow's ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles.

The support has helped keep Russia's economy and war machine operating, Montgomery argued.

In return, he said, Moscow is increasingly providing Beijing with military technology it had previously been reluctant to share — including the alleged submarine-quieting assistance.

In October 2024, the Treasury Department said a Russian defense firm coordinated production of Garpiya attack drones at factories in China, using Chinese-made engines and components before the weapons were transferred to Russia for use in Ukraine.

Russia has provided Beijing with more direct military assistance as well. A 2025 RUSI investigation, based on leaked Russian contracts and correspondence, found that Moscow agreed to equip and train a Chinese airborne battalion and transfer technology that could help Beijing develop similar capabilities itself.

Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine is now in its fifth year, with no ceasefire agreement in place despite continued diplomatic efforts. The prolonged war has deepened Moscow's dependence on Chinese industrial and financial support while giving Russia battlefield experience and military technologies that could be valuable to Beijing in a future Taiwan contingency.

For the U.S., the stakes are particularly acute around Taiwan. American submarines are central to U.S. planning for a potential Indo-Pacific conflict, and quieter Chinese vessels could make it harder to track, deter and counter the People's Liberation Army Navy in waters surrounding the island.

Montgomery said the possible transfer reflects the broader argument of "Axis of Aggressors," America's adversaries are increasingly trading the capabilities each lacks, creating challenges that span Europe and the Indo-Pacific.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Russian embassy for comment. U.S. Indo-Pacific Command declined to comment.

title: Xavi becomes first non-Dutch Netherlands coach since 1978
description: Former Barcelona manager Xavi is appointed as the new head coach of the Netherlands on a four-year deal.
fullText:
Former Barcelona manager Xavi has been appointed the new head coach of the Netherlands on a four-year deal.

The 46-year-old, who played for Barcelona and Spain, will become the first non-Dutch coach to take charge of the Netherlands since Austrian coach Ernst Happel stepped down in 1978.

Ronald Koeman resigned as Netherlands manager following a last-32 defeat by Morocco at this summer's World Cup.

"I consider it a tremendous honour to become head coach of the Dutch national team," Xavi said.

"As someone who received his training at Barca's academy, with strong influences from Johan Cruyff and Rinus Michels, among others, I feel a special connection to Dutch football.

"You could say that I am partly a son of Dutch football. Other great coaches, especially Louis van Gaal, under whom I made my debut at Barca, and Frank Rijkaard, also played an important role in shaping me as a player and coach."

Xavi will begin his Netherland's reign against Jurgen Klopp's Germany on 24 September in the Nations League.

Former Liverpool head coach Arne Slot confirmed he held talks over the job but withdrew because he wants his next role to be in club football.

Xavi, who won three international trophies, was part of the Spain team that beat the Netherlands in the 2010 World Cup final.

He retired in 2019 and went into management with Al-Sadd before taking over at Barca in November 2021, where he won a La Liga title in his first full season in charge.

It will be Xavi's first managerial job since he stepped down from Barcelona in 2024.

title: Everyone wants to 'tax the rich.' In New York City, it's getting complicated
description: Across the U.S., calls to “tax the rich” have become potent political slogans.  “It seems very simple but the more you dig into it, the more nuances you look at, the more complicated it gets,” said Ga...
fullText:
NEW YORK (AP) — Across the U.S., calls to "tax the rich" have become potent political slogans. But even in Mayor Zohran Mamdani's New York, getting the wealthy to pay more isn't playing out as smoothly as supporters hoped.

What seemed at first like an easy idea — slapping a new tax on people who own luxury second homes in the Big Apple but live elsewhere most of the year — has instead created a lot of confusion in the city's notoriously convoluted world of real estate arrangements.

"It seems very simple but the more you dig into it, the more nuances you look at, the more complicated it gets," said Gary Bingel, a state and local tax expert and partner at EisnerAmper, an accounting firm.

It has also prompted pushback from both the city's very wealthy and the merely moderately wealthy.

President Donald Trump, whose gilded Manhattan penthouse could be subject to the tax since his primary residence is now in Florida, said he was looking into whether federal intervention could "avert this disaster, before it is too late."

A group of homeowners sued over the city's rollout of the tax, arguing that officials had not done enough to figure out who would have to pay the tax and instead made it property owners' responsibility. A judge temporarily paused the process this week, but the city moved to appeal, allowing the tax effort to continue until it's sorted out in court.

Securing a new tax on multimillion-dollar second homes, known as pied-à-terres, was an early win for Mamdani in his quest to raise taxes on the city's highest earners to pay for his ambitious liberal agenda.

The so-called pied-à-terre tax would levy a new surcharge on one-, two- and three-family homes valued at more than $5 million, as well as condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more, if those dwellings are not a person's primary residence.

The idea, according to officials, would bring $500 million to the city's coffers annually, paid primarily by bigwigs who get to enjoy city life but don't pay city income taxes.

That's where things start to get hairy.

It's common for high rollers to place their properties in trusts, obscuring ownership while allowing the property to pass more easily to family members. Limited liability companies can similarly shield an owner's identity, also making it hard for government officials to tell who actually lives in any given apartment.

From there, there are numerous arrangements that can complicate who would be subject to the tax. For example, letting a distant family member stay at a second home without formal documentation, or if someone owns one or more properties and rents them out, but the tenants don't have documentation that the unit is their primary residence.

"Those situations make it difficult to prove people are in there," said Mark Limardo, a partner at the law firm Herrick in Manhattan who focuses on taxes. "The concept is simple, but the ownership rules and the documentation rules have made it very complicated."

City Hall, for its part, argues that it shouldn't be difficult to provide proof that someone actually lives in the city and says that its finance department is experienced in parsing tangled webs of paperwork.

Mamdani, no stranger to razzing wealthy people, debuted the tax with a video singling out hedge fund CEO Ken Griffin by standing outside a Manhattan penthouse the billionaire purchased for around $239 million. The clip sent Mamdani's supporters swooning, but Griffin later said it was "frightening" that a public official would call attention to one of his homes, especially after the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in the same neighborhood.

The city then published an expansive online list of property owners who it said could be subject to the tax, listing their names, addresses and property values. The list, which the city is legally required to publish, inflamed tensions between the mayor and the city's wealthy, many of whom argued the roll amounted to doxing or public shaming.

The administration has mailed notices to a much smaller group — about 17,000 properties — that it suspected would be subject to the tax, telling them they could apply for exemptions. Mamdani announced the mailers in a celebratory social media post that read: "If you have a second home in New York City worth more than $5M, check your mailbox when you're back in the five boroughs — because you've got mail."

He later pushed back the deadline for exemption requests following public outcry from people who claimed to have received the letters in error or had trouble navigating the process.

Stewart Sterk, a real estate law professor at Cardozo School of Law in New York, predicted last week's lawsuit wouldn't be the last, saying he expected many of the targets of the tax to file individual cases over denied exemptions, given the vast number of apartments at play and the various arrangements people have connecting them to their properties.

"This is going to be a subject of litigation for quite a while," he said.

title: Defense in Charlie Kirk's killing say shooter should not get death penalty, hit 'intended target'
description: The man charged with killing Charlie Kirk shouldn’t get the death penalty because the shooter “hit the intended target” and no one else was endangered when the conservative activist was shot from a ro...
fullText:
The man charged with killing Charlie Kirk shouldn't get the death penalty because the shooter "hit the intended target" and no one else was endangered when the conservative activist was shot from a rooftop at an event in Utah last year, his lawyers said.

Defendant Tyler Robinson's attorneys say the bullet traveled above the crowd of several thousand people at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10 and "there were no threats to others." Whether the shooting endangered the crowd is a key issue: Prosecutors cited the risk that other people could have been harmed as an aggravating factor under state law that makes Kirk's killing a capital crime.

"The only evidence presented supports that the bullet traveled above, not through, the crowd," defense attorneys wrote in documents filed late Tuesday as the defense tries to block the case from proceeding to trial.

Prosecutors have said numerous people were within a "zone of danger" around Kirk, where a stray or ricocheting bullet could have hurt anyone close to the victim.

The defense lawyers also disputed claims that Robinson targeted Kirk over his political views. Prosecutors allege Robinson told his roommate that he killed the activist because he "had enough of his hatred." But the defense said that was not enough to prove what motivated Robinson, after searches of his apartment, computers and telephone failed to produce anything beyond that one statement.

Prosecutors last month during a weeklong hearing presented what they call "overwhelming" evidence against Robinson, including DNA tests that tie him to the suspected murder weapon and apparent confessions by the defendant.

His attorneys questioned the reliability of the DNA tests and other evidence. They didn't offer any alternative theories for Kirk's assassination, and made no mention of DNA in Tuesday's filing.

Robinson is charged with aggravated murder and has not yet entered a plea. He turned himself in a day after Kirk was killed.

His defense attorneys previously tried to get the death penalty taken off the table after prosecutors were found to be in contempt of court for talking about the case to the media. State District Judge Tony Graf rejected that request.

In documents filed last month, prosecutors said the fact that Robinson loaded his rifle with four bullets showed that he knew he could miss Kirk, "thereby putting others in danger."

But defense attorneys said "it is just as likely that the shooter did not believe he would miss."

Robinson faces possible sentence enhancements if prosecutors can prove he targeted Kirk because of his politics. They contend that Kirk's strong opposition to same-sex marriage and gender transitioning stood in contrast to Robinson, who was in a romantic relationship with a roommate, Lance Twiggs. Twiggs told investigators that he had been considering transitioning around the time that Kirk was killed, according to prosecutors.

Twiggs also told investigators that Robinson sometimes talked about politics, including President Donald Trump. Yet Twiggs said he never heard Robinson talk about Kirk before the shooting. The defendant also did not talk much about gender issues or LGBTQ+ rights, Twiggs said. The AP emailed Twiggs' attorney seeking comment.

Closing arguments in the preliminary hearing are scheduled for Sept. 1. Graf will then decide if the case can go to trial and on what charges. Lawyers for Kirk's family have asked Graf to make his decision by or on Sept. 1 so the case can proceed.

Prosecutors have until Aug. 18 to respond to the latest defense arguments. The Associated Press left telephone and email messages with the Utah County Attorney's Office seeking comment.

Preliminary hearings typically don't last so long. Legal experts said the slow pace reflects a cautious approach by Graf, the large volume of evidence and a desire by prosecutors to disprove conspiracy theories around the case.

title: Rybakina comeback knocks Osaka out of Canadian Open
description: Elena Rybakina comes back from a set and a break down to beat Naomi Osaka in three sets in their Canadian Open quarter-final.
fullText:
Elena Rybakina came back from a set and a break down to beat Naomi Osaka in three sets in their Canadian Open quarter-final.

Four-time Grand Slam winner Osaka had won the first set and was 4-2 up in the second before her Kazakh rival came back to win 4-6 7-6 (7-5) 6-4 in two hours and 33 minutes.

"I was just trying to fight," said Rybakina, whose 72 unforced errors were her most in a match this season.

"The first game was really tough because it cost me the set, and then in the second I was just trying to stay closer to the score, even if I'm losing. I'm super happy that I won this match."

Japan's Osaka broke Rybakina in the opening game on the way to claiming the first set in Toronto.

The second set appeared to be going Osaka's way as, despite having one break retrieved, she broke again to go 4-2 up against the the 2022 Wimbledon and 2026 Australian Open champion.

However, Rybakina took three straight games and won the tie-break to level the match.

Osaka had four break points when she led 3-2 in the decider but failed to take them as Rybakina held and then broke her opponent in the next game.

Rybakina went on to emphatically serve out for the match, sealing victory with a 15th ace and she will play Coco Gauff in the semi-finals.

Meanwhile, Osaka said she was withdrawing from the Cincinnati Open, the last tournament before the US Open, because of "fatigue".

Gauff progressed after Belinda Bencic withdrew from their match with a hip injury.

The other semi-final will be between Iga Swiatek, a 6-2 6-1 winner against Diana Shnaider, and Elina Svitolina, who beat Ekaterina Alexandrova 3-6 6-0 6-3.

title: Lukaku seals 'emotional' move to Fenerbahce
description: Belgium striker Romelu Lukaku has joined Turkish side Fenerbahce from Napoli for an undisclosed fee and contract length.
fullText:
Belgium striker Romelu Lukaku has joined Turkish side Fenerbahce from Napoli.

The 33-year-old struggled with injuries last season and made only seven appearances in all competitions for the Serie A side.

Belgium's record goalscorer returns to Turkey where he lived during the 1996-1997 season when his father Roger was playing professionally for the Super Lig club Genclerbirligi.

"It's an honour and a privilege to be joining your club ," said Lukaku in a video on social media addressed to Fenerbahce's fans.

"I am fit, 100%, ready to go. It is an emotional moment after many years to be going back to Turkey where I lived as a young kid, where I discovered the professional world as a toddler with my dad."

The fee and length of contract for Lukaku has not been disclosed.

Despite an injury-hit campaign last season, the former Chelsea, Everton and Manchester United forward scored three goals at this summer's World Cup.

Lukaku has won the Belgian championship with Anderlecht, a Fifa Club World Cup with Chelsea, and a Scudetto with both Inter Milan and Napoli.

He is the second former United forward to join the club this summer after Mason Greenwood was signed from Marseille.

Fenerbahce, who have finished runners-up to Galatasaray for the last four seasons, are without a Turkish league title since 2014.

(NewsNation) — Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) has moved ahead of California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) in early prediction-market odds for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

As of Wednesday, Ocasio-Cortez had an 18 percent chance of winning the Democratic nomination on Polymarket, narrowly ahead of Newsom at 17 percent.

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) ranked third at about 16 percent, according to the data.

The New York Democrat has drawn increased attention this week after announcing she's freezing her eggs. She has also been documenting the process on her social media, which received mixed reactions.

title: Solar eclipse distracts from sporting events - in pictures
description: Pictures from sporting events as the most significant solar eclipse since 1999 is visible across the UK and Europe on Wednesday.
fullText:
The most significant solar eclipse since 1999 was visible across the UK and Europe on Wednesday and briefly took attention away from various sporting events in the process.

A total solar eclipse peaked in parts of Spain and Iceland.

In the UK, people could see a partial eclipse with more than 90% of the Sun covered by the Moon depending one where you were.

Whether you were at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham, a Hundred cricket match or Aston Villa's Super Cup game against Paris St-Germain in Austria, sports fans paused to take in the rare sight.

Experts told watchers not to look directly at the Sun without protection, which saw many supporters who did not have glasses come up with home-made solutions.

title: Jaissle 'aware' of Newcastle needs after Everton friendly loss
description: Matthias Jaissle says he is "aware" of Newcastle's shortcomings after a comfortable 3-1 friendly defeat by Everton.
fullText:
The stadium announcer at the home of Scottish rugby was certainly excited.

"Expect passion and world-class football from the very first whistle," he roared before Newcastle United met Everton in a pre-season friendly at Murrayfield.

However, pre-season, or not, this was always going to be a useful exercise for new Newcastle head coach Matthias Jaissle, as he came up against top-flight opposition just a week and a half before the new campaign starts.

The 3-1 defeat certainly served as a reminder of the work that is still required, not only on the training pitches but in the transfer market, too.

"You all see the matches," he said. "You are also smart enough to see the needs in the squad.

"I will be always consistent with my approach. We handle these things internally. We are aware of what we need. Let's see now. There is still some time."

There was a fresh look to this Newcastle side in the opening stages and fearless new signing Bazoumana Toure again caught the eye with his pace down the left.

However, Jaissle's team were unable to capitalise on a bright start - spurning a number of opportunities in front of goal - and they looked increasingly vulnerable at the back as the first half wore on.

A simple long ball forward from James Tarkowski caused havoc in the build-up to Everton's opener in the 27th minute after Thierno Barry nipped in ahead of shaky Newcastle centre-back Sven Botman to race clear.

Although Lewis Hall got back to make a recovery tackle, he could only hook the ball away as far as Harrison Armstrong, who coolly picked out Barry to finish past goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek from inside the box.

Jaissle punched the palm of his hand in frustration on the touchline before gesturing to his players to go again, just as they did when they came from behind to beat Valencia 2-1 in his first friendly at the weekend.

But Iliman Ndiaye doubled Everton's lead from the penalty spot a few minutes later after Joelinton was rather harshly adjudged to have fouled Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall inside the box.

That was the cue for taunts of "going down, going down, going down" from Everton supporters.

Once Tyrique George made it 3-0, with a drilled effort in the 73rd minute, a number of Newcastle fans started to make their way for the exit - and not to catch a glimpse of the solar eclipse.

However, there was still time for substitute Harvey Barnes to pull one back after he slammed the ball home at the back post from Jacob Murphy's cross.

Barnes and Murphy also featured when Newcastle tasted defeat against Everton in the Premier League under former head coach Eddie Howe back in February.

But this was a drastically different starting line-up following a summer of change on Tyneside.

Eight of the starters were aged 25 and under while Joelinton, who wore the captain's armband, and Yoane Wissa were the oldest by a considerable distance at 29.

Newcastle still have important figures like Dan Burn, Lewis Miley and Tino Livramento to return - albeit the trio are unlikely to all feature in the season opener versus Liverpool - but this squad clearly needs further reinforcements in the transfer market.

That won't come as news to sporting director Ross Wilson, who was among those watching on at Murrayfield on Wednesday night, or Jaissle.

It was rather telling that the German again referenced a "vacuum" for the second time in two days following the departures of Bruno Guimaraes, Sandro Tonali, Anthony Gordon and Kieran Trippier earlier this summer.

"You cannot change things really quickly," he said. "It's a really young team at the moment so there are vacuums where players need to step up.

"We fill these positions we lost with the experienced players, but that's also the process."

Newcastle remain in the market for a right-back, an older central midfielder and, depending on Jaissle's assessment of the squad, potentially another addition beyond that before the window shuts on 1 September.

There are still a couple of friendlies to play before Liverpool visit St James' Park next week, but there is little time to waste.

"If you make new signings at the end of the transfer window, they usually need time," Jaissle added. "Usually it takes time to adapt to the Premier League.

"Those are all things we consider, but we are all still positive. We all want to go in the right direction.

"We have these goals and there's many stones along the way thrown in that path, but we need to get rid of them."
